stem: A newborn had meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) and was managed appropriately. Which of the following is a common complication?
why_right: Meconium aspiration causes hypoxia, acidosis and lung inflammation, which keep the pulmonary vascular resistance high after birth. The result is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), with right to left shunting across the foramen ovale and ductus and refractory hypoxaemia. It is the classic serious complication of MAS asked in exams.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neonatal sepsis: meconium can predispose to pneumonitis, but sepsis is not the characteristic complication of MAS. Think sepsis with maternal GBS, prolonged rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis.
C. PDA: the duct may stay open as part of PPHN shunting, but isolated PDA is a complication of prematurity, not of MAS, which affects term and post term babies.
D. Diaphragmatic hernia: a congenital structural defect present before birth, not a consequence of aspiration. It is also a cause of PPHN, not a result of MAS.
key_concept:
MAS = term or post term baby, meconium stained liquor, respiratory distress.
  • Mechanism: airway obstruction (air trapping), chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation
  • Complications: PPHN, air leak (pneumothorax), later chronic lung disease
  • CXR: patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • PPHN: hypoxaemia out of proportion to lung disease, pre/post ductal saturation gap
exam_pearl: Term baby + meconium + hypoxaemia that does not improve with oxygen = PPHN.

stem: Newborn preterm baby from a mother with a gestational diabetes came with grunting and respiratory distress. next step?
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress in an infant of a diabetic mother: think glucose, surfactant, sepsis.
  • Preterm + surfactant deficiency = RDS: CXR ground glass, air bronchograms
  • Term C-section = TTN: CXR fluid in fissures, self resolving
  • Maternal diabetes: hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant, so RDS risk even near term
  • Infant of diabetic mother: early hypoglycaemia, so bedside glucose early
  • Sepsis can mimic any of these: culture then antibiotics if risk factors
exam_pearl: "Initial" or bedside step in a baby of a diabetic mother usually means glucose; "best investigation for the cause of distress" usually means CXR.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer marked; compiler put '??' after both A (Chest x ray) and B (Blood glucose).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 5-year-old child with bronchial asthma under control with inhalers. Mother concerned about the future of her child's asthma during adulthood. Which of the following is the most likely prognosis?
OptB: Most of the children grow out of it
OptD: No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma
why_right: The child is young ("5-year-old") and the asthma is "under control with inhalers", which predicts a good outlook. Many children, especially those with milder or viral triggered wheeze, become symptom free by adolescence, so the counselling answer is that most children grow out of it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chronic lung disease: well controlled childhood asthma does not usually progress to fixed chronic lung disease; that is a risk with severe, poorly controlled disease.
C. Asthmatic during adulthood: only a minority persist into adulthood, mainly those with severe disease, atopy or parental asthma.
D. No correlation: there is a correlation; severe or atopic childhood asthma raises the chance of persistence or relapse in adult life.
key_concept:
Childhood asthma prognosis: most outgrow it.
  • Better outlook: mild disease, viral triggered wheeze, good control
  • Persistence more likely: severe disease, atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis), parental asthma, female sex
  • Relapse in adulthood is possible even after remission
exam_pearl: Mild, controlled asthma in a young child = reassure that most grow out of it; atopy and severity flip the prognosis.

stem: Test Result Normal Values Sodium 127 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 6.8 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Bicarbonate 15 21-28 mmol/L Glucose 2.5 2.8-5 mmol/L. (Newborn) 3.3 -5.5 mmol/L (Child) Which of the following is the inheritance of this disease?
why_right: The labs show a salt wasting crisis: "Sodium 127", "Potassium 6.8", low bicarbonate (acidosis) and "Glucose 2.5" in a newborn. This is the picture of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (salt wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency), where cortisol and aldosterone are both deficient. All forms of CAH are autosomal recessive enzyme defects.
why_wrong_block:
A. Multifactorial: CAH is a single gene enzyme defect, not a trait from many genes plus environment (like cleft lip or pyloric stenosis).
B. X-linked dominant: CAH genes are autosomal and both sexes are affected equally. X-linked dominant fits hypophosphataemic rickets.
C. Autosomal dominant: carrier parents are unaffected and recurrence is 25% per pregnancy, which is recessive. Dominant fits disorders like NF1.
key_concept:
Neonatal hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + acidosis + hypoglycaemia = salt wasting CAH (AR).
  • Commonest: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP21A2)
  • Clues: ambiguous genitalia in girls, raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone
  • Boys may present only with salt wasting crisis in the first weeks
  • AR: 25% recurrence, higher with consanguinity
exam_pearl: Most inborn enzyme defects are autosomal recessive; X-linked enzyme exceptions (G6PD, OTC, Fabry) are worth memorising.

stem: A 2-years-old girl who has never received any vaccinations due to her mother’s personal beliefs, was injured by a contaminated metal rod. Shortly afterward, she developed muscle spasms and convulsions. Based on her clinical presentation, which vaccine should she receive?
why_right: An unvaccinated child ("never received any vaccinations") with a wound from a "contaminated metal rod" who then develops "muscle spasms and convulsions" has tetanus. The vaccine that covers tetanus is the toxoid in DTaP, the age appropriate form under 7 years. Tetanus disease does not give immunity, so active immunisation is needed in addition to tetanus immunoglobulin and wound care.
why_wrong_block:
B. OPV: protects against poliomyelitis, which causes flaccid paralysis, not spasms; it has no role in tetanus prevention.
C. IPV: also a polio vaccine; it is part of routine catch-up but does not address tetanus.
D. Hib: prevents Haemophilus influenzae type b disease (meningitis, epiglottitis), not tetanus.
key_concept:
Tetanus prone wound in an unvaccinated child: toxoid vaccine plus tetanus immunoglobulin.
  • Under 7 years: DTaP; 7 years and older: Td or Tdap
  • Unknown or incomplete series + dirty wound: vaccine AND immunoglobulin
  • Established tetanus: immunoglobulin, metronidazole, wound debridement, supportive care
  • Recovery from tetanus does not confer immunity, so complete the vaccine series
exam_pearl: Spasms and convulsions after a dirty wound = tetanus; flaccid paralysis would point to polio.

stem: toddler pt came with SOB, and plapiation upon excersie, history reveales URTI 3 days ago, examination reveales gallop rythum, vitals were provided, high HR, what clue you into diagnosis?
why_right: Breathlessness and palpitations on exercise a few days after a viral URTI suggest viral myocarditis with heart failure. Of the findings, the one that points specifically to the heart is the "gallop rhythm" (S3), a sign of ventricular dysfunction and volume overload; it moves the diagnosis from a respiratory illness to a cardiac one.
why_wrong_block:
A. History: a recent URTI is supportive but nonspecific, since it is just as common before bronchiolitis, pneumonia or asthma flares.
B. Tachypnoea: occurs in any respiratory or cardiac illness and with fever, so it does not localise the problem to the heart.
C. Tachycardia: nonspecific (fever, anxiety, dehydration, sepsis), although tachycardia out of proportion to fever does raise suspicion of myocarditis.
key_concept:
Viral myocarditis in a child: post viral illness + heart failure signs.
  • Clues: recent viral illness, exercise intolerance, palpitations, disproportionate tachycardia
  • Heart failure signs: gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly, cardiomegaly on CXR
  • Commonest causes: enteroviruses (Coxsackie B), adenovirus
  • Workup: ECG, troponin, echocardiography
exam_pearl: The specific sign beats the sensitive one: gallop rhythm localises to the heart, tachycardia and tachypnoea do not.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. The mother reports that the child frequently complains of sore throat, nasal congestion, and fever. The child has a history of asthma, and the mother states that she uses a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer as prescribed. On examination, there is mild wheeze, sore throat, and erythema. What is the most important educational advice to give the mother?
OptC: Ensure proper use of the inhaler as prescribed
OptD: Advise giving the child vitamin C–containing juices
why_right: The child is asthmatic with "mild wheeze" during a viral URTI, a common exacerbation trigger. The key education is to keep using the inhaler properly as prescribed (correct MDI and spacer technique, adherence to the controller, reliever when needed), because poor technique or stopping treatment is the main reason for loss of control.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stop inhaler use during colds: the opposite of correct advice; colds trigger exacerbations, so the controller continues and the reliever may be needed more.
B. Avoid physical activity until adolescence: asthmatic children should be active; exercise symptoms mean control needs improving, not activity restriction.
D. Vitamin C juices: no proven benefit in preventing URTIs or asthma exacerbations; not the most important advice.
key_concept:
Asthma education priorities: technique, adherence, action plan.
  • Check inhaler and spacer technique at every visit
  • Viral URTIs are the commonest trigger of exacerbations in children
  • Continue the controller during colds; use the reliever as needed
  • Before stepping up therapy, check technique, adherence and triggers
  • Encourage normal physical activity
exam_pearl: Uncontrolled or symptomatic asthma in a child: check inhaler technique first, before changing drugs.

stem: A child presents with wheezing that worsens during feeding and crying. On examination, there is monophasic bilateral expiratory wheezing. What is the most appropriate way to advise the parents?
OptC: Reassurance that it will mostly resolve spontaneously
why_right: "Monophasic bilateral expiratory wheezing" that worsens with "feeding and crying" (states that raise intrathoracic pressure and collapse a soft airway) fits tracheomalacia. With no distress or growth problem described, the condition is self limiting as the airway cartilage matures, so the advice is reassurance that it will mostly resolve spontaneously.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nebulized bronchodilator: the noise is from airway collapse, not bronchospasm, so bronchodilators do not help. Right for asthma with polyphonic wheeze.
B. Systemic steroids: no inflammatory process to treat. Right for croup or an acute asthma exacerbation.
D. Tracheostomy: only for severe malacia with apnoea, recurrent respiratory failure or failure to thrive, none of which is described.
key_concept:
Monophasic expiratory wheeze worse with crying or feeding = tracheomalacia, reassure.
  • Worse with crying, feeding, agitation, URTIs
  • Laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor, better prone
  • Diagnosis if needed: bronchoscopy
  • Resolves by 1 to 2 years
  • Red flags needing referral: apnoea, cyanosis, failure to thrive
exam_pearl: Cyanosis (not wheeze) with feeding and crying is tetralogy of Fallot; noisy breathing with feeding and crying is malacia.

stem: A child presents with weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremors, and irritability. Laboratory investigations show elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH levels. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_right: Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor with high free T4 and suppressed TSH is primary hyperthyroidism, which in a child is almost always Graves disease. The lead-in asks for the initial treatment: an antithyroid drug, and methimazole is the drug of choice in children. A beta blocker can be added for adrenergic symptoms while methimazole takes effect, but it does not treat the gland.
why_wrong_block:
B. Levothyroxine: replaces thyroid hormone, so it would worsen thyrotoxicosis. Right for hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4).
C. Surgery: a definitive option, not the first step. Right when antithyroid drugs fail or cause serious side effects, or with a large compressive goiter, after making the child euthyroid.
D. Radioactive iodine: definitive therapy that is avoided in young children and is not first line here. Right for relapse or drug failure in older children and adults; contraindicated in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Childhood hyperthyroidism (Graves): start an antithyroid drug, keep definitive therapy for failure.
  • First line: methimazole (PTU avoided in children because of hepatotoxicity)
  • Adrenergic symptoms: add propranolol for quick relief
  • Pregnancy, first trimester: PTU preferred
  • Painful tender gland after a viral illness: subacute thyroiditis, treat with NSAIDs or steroids plus beta blocker, no antithyroid drug
  • Drug failure: radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Methimazole is first line in children and in pregnancy after the first trimester; PTU only for the first trimester or thyroid storm.

stem: A 12-year-old boy with end-stage cancer and metastases to the femur and spine has a documented do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order. What is the most appropriate management to help him at this stage?
why_right: A child with end-stage cancer and bone metastases to the femur and spine with a documented DNR is in the palliative phase: the goal is comfort, not prolonging life. Bone metastases cause severe pain, and opioids such as morphine are the mainstay of pain and dyspnea control at the end of life. DNR limits resuscitation only; it never means withholding symptom relief.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inotropic support: a resuscitative, life-prolonging measure for shock, which conflicts with the DNR and the comfort-focused goals of care.
B. Mechanical ventilation: invasive life support that the DNR plan is meant to avoid. Right for reversible respiratory failure in a patient whose goals include full treatment.
D. Nothing to do: wrong because DNR is not 'do not treat'. Palliative care (analgesia, comfort, family support) continues and is actively needed here.
key_concept:
DNR = no CPR or escalation, but full symptom control.
  • Bone metastasis pain: opioids (morphine) as the core analgesic
  • End-of-life dyspnea: opioids also relieve breathlessness
  • Avoid life-prolonging interventions that conflict with goals of care (inotropes, ventilation)
  • Support the family alongside the child
exam_pearl: 'Nothing to do' is never right in palliative care: a DNR patient still gets analgesia and comfort measures.

stem: 6 weeks infant complaining of forceful vomiting after each meal, poor weight gain and dehydration. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 6-week-old with forceful vomiting after each meal, poor weight gain and dehydration is the classic picture of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Abdominal ultrasound is the first and most appropriate imaging study: it shows the thickened, elongated pylorus, is diagnostic and avoids radiation.
why_wrong_block: A. Barium study: an upper GI contrast series can show the 'string sign', but it uses radiation and is second line. Right when ultrasound is equivocal or unavailable, or when malrotation or reflux is the question.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis: projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks in a hungry infant.
  • Exam: olive-like epigastric mass
  • Imaging: abdominal ultrasound first and diagnostic
  • Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • X-ray: single bubble
  • Management: correct fluids and electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy
  • Risk factor: first-born baby
exam_pearl: If 'correct dehydration and electrolytes' is offered as the immediate step in a dehydrated infant, it beats imaging; surgery waits until the alkalosis is corrected.

stem: 11 y o boy with sudden abdominal pain lower right quadrant physical examination unremarkable (they said that exactly) Urine dipstick: unremarkable Cbc: high WBC What the Most diagnostic test
why_right: An 11-year-old with sudden right lower quadrant pain, a high WBC and an unremarkable urine dipstick (making UTI or stone less likely) needs workup for acute appendicitis. In children, abdominal ultrasound is the imaging of choice because it is accurate and avoids radiation, so it is the most appropriate diagnostic test here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal MRI: radiation-free but slower, less available and may need sedation in children. Right as a second-line study when ultrasound is equivocal, in children or pregnancy.
B. Abdominal X-ray: low yield for appendicitis (may show a fecalith only). Right for suspected obstruction or perforation (free air).
D. Laparotomy: a treatment, not a diagnostic test. Surgery follows a confirmed diagnosis, or is done directly in a peritonitic, unstable child.
key_concept:
Appendicitis imaging depends on the patient.
  • Children and pregnant women: ultrasound first
  • Non-pregnant adults: CT is best
  • Complicated appendicitis (abscess or phlegmon, RLQ mass, prolonged course): CT regardless of age
  • Inconclusive US in pregnancy: MRI
  • Treatment: antibiotics plus appendectomy
exam_pearl: A child with a tender RLQ mass after days to weeks of pain has complicated appendicitis, and that switches the answer to CT.

stem: child 5 yrs presented w. Hx. Of pneumonia and treat as outpatient with oral abx. Then he came to ER with worsening of his condition, O2% 85, he is drowsy, has moderate - severe respiratory distress (written like this) what is next ?
why_right: This child has pneumonia that worsened despite oral antibiotics, with SpO2 85%, moderate to severe distress and, decisively, he is drowsy. Altered consciousness means impending respiratory failure and an unprotected airway, which rules out non-invasive support, so the next step is intubation and invasive ventilation. The other recall version of this card (drowsy, confused, SpO2 85 to 88% on a mask) is keyed the same way.
why_wrong_block:
B. High flow O2: suits an alert child with hypoxia and moderate distress; it does not protect the airway or rescue a drowsy child who is tiring.
C. Noninvasive ventilation: needs an alert, cooperative patient who can protect the airway. Right for an awake child (or adult) with distress or hypercapnia not settling on oxygen; drowsiness is a contraindication.
D. Oxygen via non-rebreather mask: the right first move for an alert hypoxic child, but too little when there is decreased consciousness and failure of initial therapy.
key_concept:
Escalation of respiratory support is decided by consciousness and response.
  • Alert, hypoxic: oxygen by mask, then high flow
  • Alert, cooperative, still in distress or hypercapnic: NIV
  • Drowsy, confused, lost gag reflex, secretions or aspiration risk: intubate
  • Deterioration despite maximal therapy: intubate
exam_pearl: Drowsiness in respiratory failure moves the answer from NIV to intubation; an alert patient with the same saturation gets oxygen or NIV first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another recall version: child with pneumonia on treatment, ER with no improvement, O2 sat 85 or 88% on oxygen mask, drowsy, confused; A- Non-invasive ventilation, B- Invasive ventilation (highlighted).

stem: 3 yo on diet of biscuits and milk. he is pale and lethargic: hb 67 g (n: 111-117)
highlight_terms_source: 3 yo on diet of biscuits and milk
why_right: A 3-year-old on a diet of biscuits and milk who is pale and lethargic with Hb 67 g/L has nutritional iron deficiency anemia: excess milk gives little iron, displaces iron-rich foods and can cause occult gut blood loss. Because the anemia is chronic and the child is not described as hemodynamically unstable, treatment is oral iron plus dietary correction (limit milk, add iron-rich foods) with follow-up to confirm response.
why_wrong_block: A. Blood transfusion: chronic anemia is well compensated even at low Hb, and transfusion carries risks. Right when there is hemodynamic compromise, heart failure or active bleeding.
key_concept:
Stable child with dietary IDA: oral iron and diet change, then recheck.
  • Clue: excess cow's milk, little red meat
  • Labs: low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin, high TIBC, often reactive thrombocytosis
  • First line: oral ferrous sulfate
  • Parenteral iron: malabsorption, intolerance, poor compliance
  • Transfusion: instability or heart failure, not a number alone
exam_pearl: Low Hb alone does not mean transfusion in chronic IDA; look for instability, heart failure or bleeding before choosing it.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Chronic nutritional iron deficiency anemia without instability >> oral iron + diet correction. Transfusion reserved for hemodynamic compromise.

stem: A child presents with symptoms suggestive of bronchial asthma, with episodes that worsen during upper respiratory tract infections. At this visit, the chest X-ray is normal. Which Of The Following Indicates Diagnosis Of Asthma?
OptA: Bronchial asthma increases the risk of upper respiratory tract infections.
OptB: Polyphonic wheeze occurs on exertion (not exercise)
OptC: Between attacks, the chest X-ray is normal.
why_right: Asthma is a clinical diagnosis built on recurrent, variable symptoms with typical triggers. Polyphonic (widespread, expiratory) wheeze brought on by exertion reflects variable airway narrowing and is a characteristic feature that supports asthma, alongside the episodes worsening with viral URTIs. The other statements are either false or nonspecific.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asthma increasing the risk of URTIs: the relationship runs the other way; viral URTIs trigger asthma exacerbations, asthma does not make children catch more colds.
C. Normal chest X-ray between attacks: true but nonspecific, since many conditions have a normal film. The X-ray is used to exclude alternatives (foreign body, pneumonia), not to diagnose asthma.
key_concept:
Features that support childhood asthma.
  • Recurrent wheeze, cough and breathlessness, often worse at night
  • Triggers: exertion, viral URTI, cold air, allergens, smoke
  • Personal or family atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis)
  • Response to bronchodilator
  • Objective test when old enough: spirometry with reversibility
exam_pearl: Inspiratory wheeze or stridor that does not respond to bronchodilator is not asthma: think vocal cord dysfunction or an upper airway cause.

stem: What is the appropriate diet for a patient with phenylketonuria (PKU)?
why_right: PKU is a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine and accumulates, damaging the developing brain. Treatment is lifelong dietary restriction of phenylalanine using a phenylalanine-free medical formula, with tyrosine supplied because it becomes essential.
why_wrong_block:
B. Restrict fat: fat metabolism is not affected in PKU. Fat restriction or modification belongs to disorders such as long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects.
C. Restrict protein, lactose, and fructose: mixes several different diseases. Lactose (galactose) is removed in galactosemia, fructose in hereditary fructose intolerance; lactose and fructose are irrelevant in PKU.
key_concept:
Match the metabolic disease to the nutrient removed.
  • PKU: restrict phenylalanine, supplement tyrosine, avoid aspartame
  • Galactosemia: remove galactose and lactose
  • Hereditary fructose intolerance: remove fructose, sucrose, sorbitol
  • Maple syrup urine disease: restrict branched-chain amino acids
exam_pearl: In PKU the problem is one amino acid: the diet removes phenylalanine, not all protein, and adds tyrosine.

stem: pediatric with cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis and hepatic encephalopathy (confusion not stated in the stem of the question). What to avoid in diet?
why_right: This recall's key is proteins, following the classic teaching that dietary protein is broken down to ammonia in the gut, and ammonia drives hepatic encephalopathy in a cirrhotic liver that cannot clear it. On that reasoning, protein is the nutrient to limit, while fat and carbohydrate are energy sources that do not raise ammonia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fat: not linked to ammonia or encephalopathy. In cholestatic children fat is often given as medium-chain triglycerides to improve absorption and calories, not avoided.
C. Carbohydrates: the main energy source in cirrhosis; restricting them promotes muscle breakdown and hypoglycemia, which can worsen encephalopathy.
key_concept:
Hepatic encephalopathy: reduce ammonia production and absorption.
  • Lactulose first line, rifaximin as add-on
  • Look for and treat precipitants: infection (SBP), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, sedatives
  • Avoid prolonged fasting; small frequent meals with a late-evening snack
  • Ascites: restrict sodium
exam_pearl: For ascites in cirrhosis the nutrient to restrict is sodium, not protein.

stem: Neonate with TSH 60 (normal <10) has no symptoms normal appearance, ( no history about mother) What to do?
why_right: A neonate with TSH 60 ("normal <10") has a markedly positive congenital hypothyroidism screen. Babies are usually asymptomatic and normal looking at birth because maternal T4 crosses the placenta, so "no symptoms, normal appearance" does not reassure. Thyroid hormone is critical for brain development in the first weeks, so levothyroxine is started immediately once confirmatory serum TSH and free T4 are drawn, without waiting for results or imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. Waiting a month loses irreversible neurodevelopmental time; a repeat test before treating fits only a mildly raised or borderline screening TSH, not a value of 60.
C. Thyroid ultrasound or scintigraphy can define the cause (agenesis, ectopic gland, dyshormonogenesis) but is optional and must never delay starting treatment.
key_concept:
Congenital hypothyroidism on screening: draw confirmatory serum TSH + free T4, then start levothyroxine the same day.
  • Most affected newborns look normal at birth (maternal T4 cover).
  • Late signs: prolonged jaundice, constipation, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, mottled dry skin, hypotonia.
  • Most common cause: thyroid dysgenesis.
  • Imaging (US or uptake scan) is optional and never delays therapy.
  • Goal: normalize T4 quickly to protect neurodevelopment.
exam_pearl: Normal appearance does not mean normal thyroid: a clearly high newborn TSH means treat now, not observe.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought by his parents who noticed that he refuses to walk and is unable to bear weight. On examination, bowing of both legs is noted. Which of the following best describes the expected laboratory findings?
OptA: High calcium, high phosphate, low ALP, normal Vitamin D
OptB: Low calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, low Vitamin D
OptC: High calcium, high phosphate, high ALP, low Vitamin D
OptD: Low calcium, normal phosphate, normal ALP, low Vitamin D
why_right: A 2-year-old who "refuses to walk" with "bowing of both legs" has rickets, and in a toddler the usual cause is nutritional vitamin D deficiency. Low 25-OH vitamin D reduces gut calcium absorption, giving low or low-normal calcium; secondary hyperparathyroidism then wastes phosphate in the urine (low phosphate), and the poorly mineralized growth plates raise ALP. Option B is the full deficiency profile.
why_wrong_block:
A. High calcium and phosphate with low ALP is the hypophosphatasia pattern (defective ALP); it is the opposite of nutritional rickets.
C. Vitamin D deficiency cannot raise calcium and phosphate; high calcium with high ALP fits hyperparathyroidism, which lowers phosphate, so this combination fits no rickets type.
D. Normal ALP excludes active rickets, and phosphate is low in calcipenic rickets because PTH drives renal phosphate loss.
key_concept:
Rickets labs: ALP is high in every form except hypophosphatasia.
  • Nutritional vit D deficiency: Ca normal/low, PO4 low, ALP high, PTH high, 25-OH D low.
  • Vit D dependent type I: Ca low, PO4 low, ALP high, PTH high, 1,25(OH)2 D very low.
  • X-linked hypophosphatemic: Ca normal, PO4 low, ALP high, PTH normal, vit D normal.
  • Hypophosphatasia: Ca high, PO4 high, ALP markedly low.
  • Renal osteodystrophy: Ca low, PO4 high, ALP high, PTH high.
exam_pearl: Normal calcium with low phosphate and normal PTH points to X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, not deficiency.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Rickets. Compiler's typed version: '2y old came late to her milestone, bowing of the leg, widened wrist, nutrition; which result tells us it is due to deficiency? I chose: Low calcium low phosphate low 25-hydroxycholecalciferol high alkaline phosphatase'. Another version: infant cannot walk, bowed legs; options A. Normal calcium, low phosphorus; B. Low calcium, low phosphorus, high, low 25 hydroxy calciferol; C. Low calcium, low alkaline phosphate. The 'Full recall' version (used here) highlights B.

stem: Infant presents with a 3 day history of nasal congestion cough and poor feeding, On examination the infant is alert and conscious but has tachypnea and nasal flaring. ( he was in resp distress) Oxygen saturation is 89% Auscultation reveals bilateral crackles and wheezing What is the most appropriate initial management ?
OptA: Empirical antibiotics and chest Xray to rule out pneumonia
OptB: High-flow oxygen and supplemental nutrition (I don't remember if it written NGT or not )
OptC: Low-flow oxygen and IV fluids , and suction
highlight_terms_source: nasal congestion cough and poor feeding
why_right: Nasal congestion and cough for 3 days followed by tachypnea, nasal flaring, "bilateral crackles and wheezing" in an infant is bronchiolitis. Care is supportive: SpO2 89% needs supplemental oxygen, which starts as low-flow; "poor feeding" with respiratory distress needs fluid support (IV or NG); and nasal suctioning clears the blocked nose that infants depend on for breathing and feeding. The infant is "alert", so escalation is not the first step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchiolitis is viral and clinically diagnosed; routine chest X-ray and antibiotics are not indicated and are kept for suspected bacterial pneumonia, focal findings or atypical deterioration.
B. High-flow nasal oxygen is the step up when low-flow oxygen fails to correct hypoxia or work of breathing worsens; it is not the initial step in an alert infant.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = supportive care: oxygen, hydration, nasal suction.
  • Typical: infant, coryza then cough, crackles and wheeze, usually RSV.
  • Admit for low SpO2, marked tachypnea or distress, poor feeding, apnea.
  • Oxygen ladder: low-flow, then high-flow, then CPAP or ventilation.
  • Feeding support: NG or IV fluids when oral intake is poor.
  • No routine CXR, antibiotics, steroids or bronchodilators.
exam_pearl: Wheeze in an infant with coryza is bronchiolitis, not asthma: salbutamol and steroids do not change the course.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Bronchiolitis. Compiler's typed version: '3 m baby with cough and nasal congestion, low oral intake, bilateral wheeze, tachypnic but alert, O2 89%' with options A- high flow nasal O2 with IV fluid; B- IV antibiotic with xray to rule out pneumonia; C- salbutamol via spacer then reassess; D- low oxygen, frequent nasal suctioning, facilitate proper feeding (D highlighted). Fuller 'Q:' restatement on next page highlights C (low-flow oxygen, IV fluids, suction); both endorse the same approach.

stem: A term baby delivered by cesarean section, started to be tachypneic with nasal flaring and expiratory grunting. Chest X-ray showed fluid in the horizontal fissure. Blood pressure 60/35 mmHg, Heart rate 140 /min, Respiratory rate 65 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 92 %. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The clues are a "term baby delivered by cesarean section" with tachypnea, nasal flaring and grunting, only mild hypoxia (SpO2 92%), and a chest X-ray showing "fluid in the horizontal fissure". This is transient tachypnea of the newborn: delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, which is more common after cesarean delivery without labour. It is usually self-limiting within a few days with supportive care and oxygen as needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumonia needs infection risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis) or signs of sepsis, and the X-ray would show consolidation or infiltrates rather than fissural fluid; this baby is afebrile (36.6 °C) and no risk factors are given.
B. Meconium aspiration needs meconium-stained liquor, typically in a post-term or distressed baby, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on X-ray; none of that is described.
C. RDS is a disease of preterm infants with surfactant deficiency, showing a diffuse ground-glass (reticulogranular) pattern with air bronchograms and worsening distress; this is a term baby with fissural fluid.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress: match the baby and the X-ray.
  • TTN: term, cesarean, fluid in fissures/perihilar streaks, resolves within days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground-glass with air bronchograms
  • Meconium aspiration: post-term, meconium liquor, patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • Pneumonia: maternal fever/PROM, consolidation, signs of sepsis
exam_pearl: Same symptoms in a 27-week preterm with low saturations flips the answer to RDS; "term + cesarean + fissure fluid" is TTN.

stem: Cystic fibrosis complain of weight 3rd centile Inability to gain weight Foul smelling stool What health promotion you can offer
why_right: In cystic fibrosis, weight at the 3rd centile, "inability to gain weight" and "foul smelling stool" mean steatorrhea from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts so fat and protein are not digested. Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals and snacks treats the cause and restores weight gain.
why_wrong_block:
B. A high-fiber diet adds bulk without calories and does not correct fat malabsorption; weight gain in CF needs more absorbable calories, not more fiber.
C. CF children need a high-calorie, high-fat diet; fat is restricted only in disorders such as chylous effusions or some fat oxidation defects, never as CF management.
D. Fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) supplements are part of CF care, but they are added alongside enzymes and do not correct the steatorrhea or weight faltering.
key_concept:
CF with steatorrhea and failure to thrive: pancreatic enzyme replacement with every meal and snack.
  • Diet: high calorie, high fat, extra salt.
  • Add fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K.
  • GI features: meconium ileus, steatorrhea, rectal prolapse, distal intestinal obstruction.
  • Poor weight gain separates CF from asthma in a wheezy child.
exam_pearl: Low-fat diet is the classic trap: CF needs more fat and calories, made absorbable by enzymes.

stem: 10 years child with drooling, ptosis dysartheria at evening only, he is normal in the morning, neurological exam revealed exuasting ptosis and mild dysartheria Which is a test to confirm?
highlight_terms_source: at evening only, he is normal in the morning
why_right: Ptosis, drooling and dysarthria that appear "at evening only" and are "normal in the morning", with fatigable ptosis on exam, are fluctuating bulbar and ocular weakness: myasthenia gravis. The disease is caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, so the serum AChR antibody test is the confirmatory test.
why_wrong_block:
A. Muscle biopsy is for myopathies and dystrophies with fixed proximal weakness; the muscle itself is normal in myasthenia.
B. Routine nerve conduction is normal in myasthenia; it confirms neuropathies such as GBS. Only repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG shows the decrement, and that is a supporting test when antibodies are negative.
C. CK is normal in myasthenia; it is raised in muscular dystrophy (e.g. Duchenne) and inflammatory myositis.
key_concept:
Fatigable weakness worse later in the day with normal reflexes and sensation = myasthenia gravis.
  • Confirm: AChR antibodies (anti-MuSK if negative).
  • Electrophysiology: decrement on repetitive stimulation, jitter on single-fiber EMG.
  • Bedside: ice pack test, edrophonium test.
  • Look for thymoma with chest CT.
  • Treat: pyridostigmine; IVIG or plasma exchange in crisis.
exam_pearl: Worse in the evening and better after rest is MG; weakness that improves with repeated effort suggests Lambert-Eaton.

What to do next' with options Nerve conduction / Muscle biopsy / Acetylcholine receptor antibody (highlighted) / 'Forgot, viral testing maybe?'. Fuller 'Q:' version used here.

stem: Child with seizures Anti ds DNA high ANA normal What to give ?
key_concept:
SLE drug choice follows the organ and the severity.
  • All patients: hydroxychloroquine.
  • Mild (skin, joints): HCQ + NSAID, then low-dose steroid + methotrexate.
  • Life-threatening: high-dose steroid + immunosuppressant.
  • Neuropsychiatric: cyclophosphamide.
  • Nephritis: mycophenolate mofetil.
  • Seizures in SLE: exclude infection, electrolytes and drugs first.
exam_pearl: "Initial" in severe lupus points to steroids; "add to steroids" for CNS lupus points to cyclophosphamide.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for pallor and easy fatigability since early childhood. He has no history of bleeding. On examination: mild splenomegaly. CBC: Hb = 8 g/dL; MCV = 62 fL; RBC count = normal to high. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous target cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: pallor and easy fatigability since early childhood
why_right: Pallor "since early childhood" with mild splenomegaly, a very low MCV (62) out of proportion to the anemia, a "normal to high" RBC count and "numerous target cells" is the thalassemia pattern. The marrow makes many small, poorly hemoglobinized cells (high RBC count, Mentzer index below 13), and chronic extravascular hemolysis enlarges the spleen. Hemoglobin electrophoresis (raised HbA2 and HbF) confirms beta thalassemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Iron deficiency also causes microcytosis, but the RBC count falls with it (Mentzer above 13), target cells are not prominent and splenomegaly is not expected; in a child it usually follows a poor diet such as excess cow's milk, with low ferritin.
B. Anemia of chronic disease needs an underlying chronic illness, is usually normocytic or mildly microcytic, has high ferritin and no splenomegaly or target cells.
C. Sideroblastic anemia shows ringed sideroblasts on marrow and high iron; it is rare in children and has no high RBC count or prominent target cells.
key_concept:
Microcytic anemia: separate by RBC count, iron studies and electrophoresis.
  • Thalassemia: RBC count normal or high, Mentzer (MCV/RBC) below 13, target cells, raised HbA2.
  • Iron deficiency: low RBC count, Mentzer above 13, low ferritin, high RDW.
  • Chronic disease: high ferritin, low TIBC.
  • Sideroblastic: ringed sideroblasts, high iron.
  • Failure to respond to iron points to thalassemia.
exam_pearl: Very low MCV with a high RBC count is thalassemia until proven otherwise; iron deficiency drops the RBC count.

stem: Foul smelling watery diarrhea, green in color, what is the causative organism?
highlight_terms_source: Foul smelling watery diarrhea, green in color
key_concept:
Diarrhea description to organism.
  • Green, foul, slimy (pea soup): Salmonella.
  • Bloody mucoid with seizure: Shigella.
  • Profuse watery with vomiting in infants: Rotavirus.
  • Rice-water, painless, huge volume: Vibrio cholerae.
  • Chronic watery with weight loss after travel: Giardia.
  • Vomiting a few hours after a meal: Staphylococcus aureus toxin.
exam_pearl: The color word decides it: "green, foul" is the Salmonella descriptor, while "blood and mucus" moves to Shigella.

stem: Baby 9 month never been vaccinated what vaccines you will give :
OptD: BCG Hep B OPV-1 Dtap-1 Measles
key_concept:
Catch-up rule: give all age-appropriate vaccines at one visit, use minimum intervals, never restart a series.
  • Saudi birth: BCG, Hep B.
  • 2, 4, 6 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV13 (+ rotavirus at 2 and 4; OPV from 6).
  • 9 months: measles + MCV4.
  • 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV13, MCV4.
  • Rotavirus is not started late; MMR and varicella not before 12 months.
exam_pearl: In catch-up, pick the option that combines missed birth doses, first primary doses and age-due vaccines, not just one age slot.

stem: 5 year Pedia patient comes with fever 37.9 for 6 weeks associated with joint pain with salmon color rash especially trunk and hepatomegaly and bilateral wrist swelling What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Fever for "6 weeks" with joint pain and "bilateral wrist swelling" (arthritis lasting 6 weeks or more), a "salmon color rash especially trunk" and hepatomegaly in a 5-year-old is systemic JIA (Still disease). The evanescent salmon-pink rash that appears with fever spikes and the hepatosplenomegaly are the systemic features that separate it from other JIA subtypes. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion, so infection and malignancy must be ruled out.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kawasaki disease is fever of 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, extremity changes, polymorphous rash and cervical node; it does not cause 6 weeks of chronic wrist arthritis or a salmon rash.
B. Option not recalled; likely distractors here are acute leukemia (bone pain, cytopenias, night pain) or acute rheumatic fever (migratory large-joint arthritis after strep throat), both important exclusions in this picture.
C. Option not recalled; another common distractor is SLE, which in children shows malar rash, oral ulcers, cytopenias and renal involvement rather than a salmon fever rash.
key_concept:
JIA = arthritis 6 weeks or more, onset before 16, others excluded.
  • Systemic: age 2 to 4, quotidian fever, salmon rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis.
  • Oligoarticular: under 6, 1 to 4 large joints, asymptomatic uveitis.
  • Polyarticular: 5 or more joints, symmetric.
  • Complication of systemic JIA: macrophage activation syndrome.
  • Exclude leukemia and infection first.
exam_pearl: Salmon rash that comes with the fever and fades with it is systemic JIA; a short fever with mucocutaneous signs is Kawasaki.

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents to the clinic complaining of abdominal pain, frequent diarrhoea that is sometimes bloody, and pain usually accompanying defecation. His mother observed that he has lost weight over the last 3 months since the onset of the problem. The boy also has aches and pains of his joints. On examination, he looks ill, pale, with a sol abdomen, no tenderness or organomegaly (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mm Heart rate 100/min Respiratory rate 16/min Temperature 38.6° C. Sodium 132 (134-146 mmol/L), Potassium 3.2 (3.5-5.1 mmol/L), Creatinine 31 (27-62), BUN 5.6 (1.8-6.4 mmol/L), Hb 82 (112-165 g/L), C-reactive peptide 1.1 (0-0.5 mg/dl), Albumin 32 (36-52 g/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clues are diarrhoea that is "sometimes bloody" with "pain usually accompanying defecation" (rectal and colonic inflammation causing urgency and tenesmus). "Aches and pains of his joints" is a classic extra-intestinal manifestation of IBD, and fever, anaemia (Hb 82), hypoalbuminaemia, raised CRP and weight loss over 3 months confirm a chronic active inflammatory colitis. Bloody diarrhoea plus IBD features points to ulcerative colitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Celiac disease gives non-bloody, malabsorptive diarrhoea with distension and failure to thrive; it does not cause fever, raised CRP or bloody stools. Right when the child has steatorrhoea after gluten introduction with positive tTG IgA.
B. Crohn's disease classically gives non-bloody diarrhoea, RLQ pain or mass, oral ulcers and perianal disease (fistula, skin tags) with marked growth failure; visible blood with painful defecation favours UC here.
D. Chronic dysentery (e.g., amoebic colitis or persistent bacterial infection) needs an exposure or travel history and positive stool microscopy or culture, and does not explain arthralgia with this inflammatory picture; stool studies are still sent to exclude infection before labelling IBD.
key_concept:
Chronic bloody diarrhoea + extra-intestinal features in a child = IBD; blood favours UC.
  • UC: bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus, continuous colonic disease from the rectum
  • Crohn's: non-bloody diarrhoea, RLQ pain, oral ulcers, perianal disease, skip lesions
  • Both: arthralgia, fever, anaemia, low albumin, weight loss
  • Celiac: non-bloody malabsorption, no fever
  • Always exclude infection with stool cultures
exam_pearl: Blood in the stool tips IBD toward UC; perianal disease, oral ulcers or a RLQ mass tip it toward Crohn's.

stem: Child with poor dentition, enamel hypoplasia, low calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: low calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase
why_right: Low calcium, low phosphate and high alkaline phosphatase with "poor dentition, enamel hypoplasia" is the biochemical picture of nutritional (vitamin D deficiency) rickets. The question asks for the "most appropriate management" of a child with no tetany or seizures described, so the treatment is oral vitamin D3 replacement together with calcium supplementation to heal the bone and teeth.
why_wrong_block: A. IV calcium gluconate is for symptomatic acute hypocalcaemia (tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, prolonged QT) or hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; it corrects the level briefly but does not treat the underlying vitamin D deficiency. Nothing acute is described here.
key_concept:
Rickets labs decide the cause and the treatment.
  • Nutritional (vitamin D deficiency): Ca low or normal, PO4 low, ALP high, PTH high: oral vitamin D + calcium
  • X-linked hypophosphataemic: Ca normal, PO4 low, ALP high, vitamin D normal: phosphate + calcitriol
  • Renal osteodystrophy: PO4 high, creatinine high
  • Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizure): IV calcium gluconate first, then vitamin D
exam_pearl: IV calcium only if the hypocalcaemia is symptomatic; otherwise treat the cause with oral vitamin D plus calcium.

stem: Newborn didn't pass meconium for 48h when examining the rectum it exploded with temporarily relieve of the symptoms. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours in a term newborn is the classic red flag for Hirschsprung disease. On rectal examination the stool and gas "exploded" out with temporary relief (the squirt or blast sign): the finger dilates the aganglionic, tight segment and releases the obstruction above it.
why_wrong_block: B. Functional constipation is a disease of older infants and children (often around toilet training) with a normal meconium history and a rectum full of hard stool; a newborn who has not passed meconium in 48 hours must be assumed to have an organic cause.
key_concept:
Delayed meconium (>24 to 48 h) + explosive stool after DRE = Hirschsprung.
  • DRE: tight sphincter, empty rectum, explosive release of stool and gas
  • Contrast enema: transition zone (narrow distal, dilated proximal)
  • Diagnosis: rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells
  • Association: Down syndrome
  • Alternatives in a neonate: meconium ileus (cystic fibrosis), meconium plug, hypothyroidism
exam_pearl: Normal meconium passage in the first 24 to 48 hours makes Hirschsprung much less likely; delayed meconium makes functional constipation the wrong answer.

stem: child with flu symptoms + trial of amoxicillin with no improvement. Mother asking about preventive measures?
why_right: "Flu symptoms" with no response to amoxicillin points to a viral respiratory infection, which antibiotics do not treat or prevent. The question asks about "preventive measures", and the evidence-based prevention for respiratory infections in children is immunisation (seasonal influenza vaccine, plus completing routine vaccines such as pneumococcal, Hib and pertussis), alongside hand hygiene.
why_wrong_block: A. Vitamin C supplements have not been shown to prevent colds or flu in the general population; at most they may modestly shorten symptom duration. It would only be right if the child had true scurvy (bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage, poor diet).
key_concept:
Viral URTI: antibiotics do not help; prevention = vaccination + hygiene.
  • Annual influenza vaccine from 6 months of age
  • Complete routine schedule (pneumococcal, Hib, pertussis, measles)
  • Hand washing, avoid smoke exposure
  • Vitamin C: no proven preventive benefit
exam_pearl: Failure of amoxicillin is a clue that the illness is viral; the preventive answer is a vaccine, not a supplement or prophylactic antibiotic.

stem: 2 years old has Aortic stenosis his parents brought him due to new progressive SOB during moderate exercise, ECHO: Moderate AS Most appropriate management?
why_right: The child has known aortic stenosis and now has "new progressive SOB during moderate exercise", i.e. the stenosis has become symptomatic. In valve disease the rule is that symptoms mandate intervention, and in children with congenital valvar AS the first-line intervention is percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty, which delays the need for surgical valve replacement in a growing child.
why_wrong_block:
B. Medications cannot relieve a fixed valvular obstruction or change prognosis in AS; they are only supportive (e.g., heart failure treatment while awaiting intervention). A child with new exertional symptoms needs the obstruction relieved.
C. Reassurance with echo follow-up is appropriate only for mild or asymptomatic AS; new progressive exertional dyspnoea is a warning sign (risk of syncope and sudden death) and needs intervention.
key_concept:
Valvular disease: asymptomatic = follow up; symptomatic = intervene.
  • Child with congenital valvar AS needing intervention: balloon valvuloplasty first
  • Adult symptomatic severe AS: surgical or transcatheter valve replacement
  • Red-flag symptoms in AS: exertional dyspnoea, syncope, chest pain
  • Medication does not relieve fixed obstruction
exam_pearl: In AS the symptom drives the decision more than the echo grade; in a child the intervention is balloon valvuloplasty, in an adult it is valve replacement.

stem: Down syndrome delivered 2 days ago, what is the recommended screening for this patient:
OptA: Serial abdominal x ray for another atresia "not duodenal"
why_right: Down syndrome is associated with Hirschsprung disease (as well as duodenal atresia, which would already be obvious with bilious vomiting and a double bubble). In a well 2-day-old after an uncomplicated delivery, the practical screen is to watch for passage of meconium in the first 24 to 48 hours; delay should prompt evaluation for Hirschsprung.
why_wrong_block:
A. Serial abdominal x-rays are not a screening tool; imaging is done only if there are signs of obstruction (bilious vomiting, distension). Duodenal atresia presents within hours with a double bubble rather than being found on routine films.
B. Pyloric stenosis presents at around 2 to 8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and is not a recognised Down syndrome screen; ultrasound is done only when symptoms suggest it.
D. The option says "necrotizing fasciitis" but means necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Fecal calprotectin is not a newborn screen (levels are physiologically high in neonates), and NEC is a clinical and radiological diagnosis (feeding intolerance, bloody stool, pneumatosis), mainly in preterm infants.
key_concept:
Down syndrome GI associations: duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease.
  • Duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting in first day, double bubble
  • Hirschsprung: delayed meconium >24 to 48 h, distension
  • Also screen: echocardiogram (AVSD), congenital hypothyroidism (TSH), hearing and eyes
  • Pyloric stenosis: 2 to 8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting
exam_pearl: Down syndrome + newborn who has not passed meconium by 48 hours = think Hirschsprung.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot version: 'A 2 day old newborn with down syndrome was born with uncomplicated labour, what should you screen for?' 1- (daily) abdominal x-ray to rule out atresia; 2- routine abdominal US to rule out pyloric stenosis; 3- fecal calprotectin to detect NEC; 4- monitor for passage of meconium (beyond) 24-48 hrs. 'Answer: D' refers to the screenshot's 4th option (monitor meconium passage), consistent with the typed highlight.

stem: Child fell down then had tonic-clonic seizure, came to the ER, drowsy but arousable, neurological exam is normal (includes pupils ... ete), best step:
OptC: Observe in the ER for 2 hours
highlight_terms_source: fell down then had tonic-clonic seizure
why_right: The child had head trauma ("fell down") followed by a tonic-clonic seizure and is still "drowsy but arousable". A post-traumatic seizure and altered level of consciousness are high-risk features for intracranial injury, so the best step is an urgent non-contrast CT head, the imaging of choice for acute bleeding, even though the neurological exam is otherwise normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Admission for observation is the plan after CT is negative or for low-to-intermediate risk head injury; it must not replace imaging when there is a seizure and drowsiness.
C. A short ER observation period suits minor head trauma with an isolated low-risk feature and normal mental status; it is unsafe when the child has seized and remains drowsy.
D. Discharge with head-injury instructions is only for low-risk minor head trauma with normal mental status and no seizure, vomiting or loss of consciousness.
key_concept:
Paediatric head injury: high-risk features = CT now.
  • High risk: seizure, altered mental status or GCS <15, focal deficit, signs of skull fracture
  • Intermediate risk: brief LOC, vomiting, severe mechanism, severe headache: observe or CT
  • Low risk: normal mental status, no red flags: discharge with instructions
  • Acute bleed imaging: non-contrast CT
exam_pearl: A normal neurological exam does not cancel the CT when the child seized after the fall and is still drowsy.

stem: A 5-year-old girl presents with fever and burning urination. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic?
why_right: A 5-year-old who can take oral medication with fever and dysuria has a UTI that can be managed as an outpatient. Oral antibiotics are as effective as parenteral therapy in a child who is not toxic or vomiting, so the key here is an oral agent, amoxicillin, rather than an injectable or a fluoroquinolone.
why_wrong_block:
B. IM ceftriaxone is a parenteral option for children who look toxic, are vomiting, cannot take oral medication, or are young infants; it is not needed for a well child with fever and dysuria.
C. IV ciprofloxacin is not first line in children (musculoskeletal adverse effects, resistance concerns) and is reserved for resistant or complicated infections; the IV route is also unnecessary here.
key_concept:
Paediatric UTI: route depends on how ill the child is, not the fever alone.
  • Well, tolerating oral: oral antibiotic per local E. coli susceptibility
  • Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated or young infant: parenteral (e.g., ceftriaxone)
  • Fluoroquinolones: avoid as first line in children
  • Always send urine culture before starting
exam_pearl: Fever alone does not mandate IV or IM therapy in a child who can drink and take tablets; toxicity or vomiting does.

stem: I remember the sucking reflex and the automatic walking reflex disappear at what age. Each question had: (this one: sucking reflex disappears at what age?)
key_concept:
Primitive reflexes: present at birth, fade in a set order.
  • ~2 months: stepping (automatic walking)
  • 2 to 3 months: ATNR
  • ~4 months: rooting, sucking, Galant
  • ~6 months: Moro, palmar grasp
  • 12 to 18 months: Babinski
  • Parachute: appears 8 to 10 months, never disappears
exam_pearl: Stepping is the earliest reflex to go (about 2 months); a persistent primitive reflex beyond its age suggests a CNS problem such as cerebral palsy.

Compiler note: Recaller says the sucking reflex and the automatic walking reflex were asked as separate questions with the same options.

stem: Long term management of X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency?
key_concept:
SCID = T-cell (and B-cell) failure; only stem cell transplant cures it.
  • X-linked SCID: IL-2 receptor common gamma chain defect, boys, severe infections and failure to thrive in infancy
  • Definitive: haematopoietic stem cell transplant
  • Bridging: IVIG, PJP prophylaxis, only irradiated CMV-negative blood products, no live vaccines
  • Bruton XLA (B-cell only): lifelong IVIG is the long-term treatment
exam_pearl: Monthly immunoglobulin is the long-term answer for Bruton agammaglobulinaemia, but for SCID it is only a bridge to bone marrow transplant.

stem: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. She is concerned of bed-wetting overnight despite toilet training and several sessions of discussion. He feels a shamed and asked help from his family and physician. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: An 11-year-old with ongoing nocturnal enuresis who is ashamed and asking for help is keyed to a comprehensive, family centred behavioural approach. In this recall's teaching ladder, behavioural therapy (family support, no blame, reward systems, voiding before bed, evening fluid habits) is first line, the enuresis alarm second, and desmopressin third. Family involvement also addresses the child's shame and keeps him motivated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Avoiding punishment is one element of the behavioural approach, not a complete management plan on its own; the family centred package includes it.
B. Desmopressin comes after behavioural measures and the alarm in this ladder, and the intranasal form is no longer used for enuresis because of hyponatraemia and seizure risk (oral tablets or melts are used). It fits when rapid short term dryness is needed, such as a sleepover or camp.
C. The bed alarm with positive reinforcement is the second step in this ladder, used when behavioural measures fail in a motivated child and family.
key_concept:
Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: reassure, then treat in steps.
  • Step 1: urinalysis in every child; classify primary vs secondary
  • Secondary: look for a stressor or new organic cause
  • First line: behavioural, family centred (no punishment, rewards, toileting, fluids)
  • Second line: enuresis alarm (needs motivated child and family)
  • Third line: oral desmopressin (fast effect, high relapse on stopping)
exam_pearl: Intranasal desmopressin is out for enuresis (hyponatraemia); if a drug option says 'intranasal', it is the trap.

stem: 10-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with polyuria, polydipsia, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and is started on IV fluids and IV insulin infusion. After 2 hours of treatment, the child becomes confused and drowsy, with a decreased level of consciousness. Vital signs are stable, and blood glucose is declining steadily. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A child with DKA who becomes confused and drowsy a few hours into fluids and insulin while glucose is declining has cerebral oedema until proven otherwise, the most feared complication of paediatric DKA treatment. It is treated immediately on clinical grounds with IV mannitol (hypertonic saline is the alternative), head elevation and reduced fluid rate, before any imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. More fluid is harmful here; overly rapid fluid replacement is linked to cerebral oedema, so the fluid rate should be reduced. Extra fluid fits shock or persistent hypovolaemia, not a falling conscious level with stable vitals.
C. Stopping insulin would let ketoacidosis rebound and does not treat raised intracranial pressure; insulin is continued, with dextrose added as glucose falls.
D. Dextrose is added to fluids when glucose falls to allow insulin to continue, but switching to dextrose fluids only does nothing for brain swelling. It would fit hypoglycaemia, which is excluded by the steadily declining but not low glucose.
key_concept:
Neurological deterioration during DKA treatment = cerebral oedema; treat at once.
  • Warning signs: headache, confusion, drowsiness, falling GCS, bradycardia with hypertension, vomiting
  • Give IV mannitol or hypertonic saline
  • Elevate head, reduce IV fluid rate
  • Check glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
  • Imaging only after treatment has started
exam_pearl: Confusion after starting DKA treatment in a child: mannitol first, CT later; do not give more fluid.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: 'Pediatric patients with DKA after corrections he becomes drowsy. How to manage? IV mannitol / IV NS bolus every 15 min. Answer: A' (IV mannitol). Better recall given as the stem.

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a barky cough, appears cyanotic, and has spells of breath-holding. On auscultation, you hear a monophasic wheeze. There is no inspiratory stridor noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A barky (brassy) cough, a monophasic expiratory wheeze, cyanotic spells and no inspiratory stridor point to an intrathoracic airway collapse: tracheomalacia. The floppy trachea collapses during expiration and coughing, giving a single pitch central wheeze and occasional cyanotic 'dying spells'. Diagnosis is by bronchoscopy, and it usually improves with growth.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchiolitis (infant under about 2 years, viral prodrome, crackles and diffuse polyphonic wheeze) and bronchitis are acute infections, not a recurrent barky cough with a fixed monophasic wheeze.
C. Laryngomalacia is supraglottic, so it causes inspiratory stridor in early infancy that worsens supine and improves prone; the stem explicitly says no inspiratory stridor.
D. Asthma gives a polyphonic, diffuse expiratory wheeze that responds to bronchodilators, not a monophasic central wheeze with a brassy barky cough.
key_concept:
Site of the airway lesion decides the noise.
  • Extrathoracic (larynx): inspiratory stridor, e.g. laryngomalacia, croup
  • Intrathoracic large airway (trachea): monophasic expiratory wheeze, barky cough, e.g. tracheomalacia
  • Small airways: polyphonic wheeze, e.g. asthma, bronchiolitis
  • Laryngomalacia diagnosis: laryngoscopy; tracheomalacia: bronchoscopy
  • Both are usually self limiting with growth
exam_pearl: Stridor on inspiration = larynx; monophasic wheeze on expiration with barky cough = trachea.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second version (Q:): 4 year old boy with barking cough, monophonic wheeze, cyanotic, no inspiratory stridor; options Bronchiolitis / Tracheomalacia / Laryngomalacia / B. asthma. Answer: Tracheomalacia.

stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to Well Baby Clinic by her mother because she is crying intensely recently and is not sleeping well overnight. The mother gave history of normal feeding. No fever or vomiting. These crying episodes are 2 to 3 min per week, last for 1 to 2 hours since the age of 1 month. Which of the following is the recommended revealing measure?
why_right: A 2-month-old with paroxysms of intense crying lasting 1 to 2 hours, a few times a week since 1 month, with normal feeding and no fever or vomiting, is a healthy infant with infantile colic. Colic is self limited, so management is supportive: reassure the parents and teach soothing strategies (holding, rocking, swaddling, white noise), i.e. behavioural adaptation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Feeding is normal and there is no vomiting, bloody stool or poor growth to suggest cow's milk protein allergy; routine formula changes are not recommended for colic.
B. Colic drops such as simethicone have no proven benefit, and anticholinergic drops are unsafe in young infants.
C. Respite may ease caregiver stress, but a baby sitter is not a treatment and does not teach the soothing and coping strategies that are the mainstay.
key_concept:
Infantile colic: healthy infant, crying paroxysms, self limited within the first months.
  • Rule of 3s: crying more than 3 h/day, more than 3 days/week, more than 3 weeks
  • Normal feeding, growth and examination; no fever or vomiting
  • Treatment: reassurance plus behavioural adaptation
  • No routine formula switch or medication
  • Red flags (fever, vomiting, poor growth) mean look for another cause
exam_pearl: Crying infant with normal feeding and growth: reassure and soothe; drugs or formula changes are the trap.

stem: Child came to the clinic regarding poor nutrition, he is always eating biscuits and milk and not eating well. On examination there is mild conjunctival pallor, Hb is 6.2 mg/dl with low MCV. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
OptB: Give oral iron and advise diet modification
highlight_terms_source: Hb is 6.2 mg/dl with low MCV
why_right: A child who lives on biscuits and milk with pallor, low Hb and low MCV has nutritional iron deficiency anaemia (excess milk is low in iron and displaces iron rich food). With only mild pallor and no signs of decompensation, the anaemia is chronic and tolerated, so treatment is therapeutic oral iron plus dietary change (limit milk, add iron rich foods) and follow-up to confirm a rise in Hb.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, heart failure or acute severe symptoms; a stable child with chronic IDA corrects well with oral iron.
C. Bone marrow aspiration is invasive and not needed for typical nutritional IDA; it fits pancytopenia, blasts or suspected leukaemia or marrow failure.
D. Folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia; here the MCV is low, and multivitamins contain too little iron to treat established anaemia.
key_concept:
Microcytic anaemia in a toddler or child with a milk heavy diet = IDA until proven otherwise.
  • Labs: low Hb, MCV, ferritin; high TIBC and RDW
  • Treat: oral ferrous sulfate plus diet change (limit cow's milk)
  • Failure to respond to adequate iron: check adherence, then Hb electrophoresis for thalassaemia
  • Transfuse only if haemodynamically unstable or in heart failure
exam_pearl: A low Hb number alone does not mean transfusion; a stable child with chronic IDA gets oral iron.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B (confirmed). Original recall: child only eating bread and milk, possible PICA, Hb 7; A blood transfusion / B Give oral iron and encourage healthy food. Embedded screenshot version (biscuits and milk, Hb 6): A. Give oral iron and encourage healthy food, B. Start blood transfusion; answer A. Give oral iron and encourage healthy food.

stem: Symptoms of pertussis. Management
key_concept:
Pertussis: catarrhal URTI phase, then paroxysmal whooping cough.
  • Paroxysms may end in cyanosis or post-tussive vomiting
  • Young infants may have apnoea instead of a whoop
  • Diagnosis: nasopharyngeal PCR (culture is the gold standard)
  • Treatment and close contact prophylaxis: macrolide
  • Contacts get prophylaxis even if vaccinated
exam_pearl: Whoop plus post-tussive vomiting = pertussis = macrolide for the patient and every household contact.
