stem: A 7-year-old child presents with pneumonia. What is the most common causative organism?
why_right: In a school-age child (7 years) with community acquired pneumonia, the most common bacterial cause is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Neonatal organisms (Group B Streptococcus, E. coli) do not apply at this age; Mycoplasma is the main atypical alternative in older children.
why_wrong_block:
A. E. coli causes neonatal sepsis and pneumonia and is the top cause of UTI, not of community acquired pneumonia in a 7-year-old.
C. Group B Streptococcus is the leading cause of neonatal pneumonia, sepsis and meningitis (first weeks of life), not school-age pneumonia.
D. E. coli (repeated option) is a neonatal and urinary pathogen, not the common cause of childhood community acquired pneumonia.
key_concept:
Pneumonia organism by age:
  • Neonate: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli and other Gram negatives
  • Infant and preschool: viruses most common overall; S. pneumoniae is the top bacterium
  • School-age: S. pneumoniae; Mycoplasma for atypical pneumonia
  • Lobar consolidation at any age beyond the neonatal period: think S. pneumoniae
exam_pearl: Neonate = GBS and E. coli; beyond the neonatal period, typical bacterial pneumonia = S. pneumoniae.

stem: 7-year-old child presented with shortness of breath. On examination, there was unilateral dullness. X-ray showed consolidations. What is the most likely causative organism?
why_right: Unilateral dullness and consolidation on X-ray in a 7-year-old describe typical lobar pneumonia, and the most common organism for community acquired lobar pneumonia in children is Streptococcus pneumoniae.
why_wrong_block:
A. Group B streptococcus is a neonatal pathogen (pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis in the first weeks of life), not a cause of pneumonia in a 7-year-old.
C. Pseudomonas causes pneumonia in cystic fibrosis, ventilated or hospitalised and immunocompromised patients, not in a previously well child with community acquired pneumonia.
D. Haemophilus influenzae type b became rare after Hib vaccination; non-typeable H. influenzae is more typical of otitis media, sinusitis and COPD exacerbations than lobar pneumonia in children.
key_concept:
Lobar consolidation in a previously well child = S. pneumoniae.
  • Signs: dullness, bronchial breathing, crackles over one area
  • Neonate: GBS, E. coli
  • School-age atypical: Mycoplasma (patchy, extrapulmonary features)
  • Cystic fibrosis or hospital acquired: Pseudomonas
  • Post-influenza or cavitating or empyema: consider S. aureus
exam_pearl: Pseudomonas needs a reason (CF, ventilator, immunosuppression); without one, lobar pneumonia is pneumococcal.

stem: Child due for vaccination has rhinitis, coryza and conjunctivitis?
why_right: A child due for vaccination with rhinitis, coryza and conjunctivitis has a minor illness. Mild illness, with or without low grade fever, is not a contraindication to live vaccines, so MMR is given on schedule to avoid missed opportunities; only moderate or severe acute illness justifies deferral.
why_wrong_block:
B. There is no reason to drop the rubella component; MMR is given as the full combined vaccine, and a cold has no bearing on any single component.
C. Skipping or deferring the dose is wrong for a minor illness and leaves the child unprotected. Deferral fits moderate or severe illness, or a true contraindication such as severe immunodeficiency or prior anaphylaxis to the vaccine.
key_concept:
Minor illness is not a reason to delay vaccines.
  • Give: URTI, mild diarrhoea, low grade fever, on antibiotics, recovering from illness
  • Defer: moderate or severe acute illness with or without fever
  • Live vaccine contraindications: severe immunodeficiency, pregnancy, prior anaphylaxis to the vaccine
  • Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR
  • Missed doses: give them now, do not restart the series
exam_pearl: Runny nose and red eyes on vaccination day: vaccinate; do not confuse a cold with a contraindication.

stem: Child in outpatient with chills, fever and +ve nitrite & leukocyte, asked about what to do next?
OptB: Refer to hospital for IV antibiotic
key_concept:
Febrile UTI in a child: route of antibiotics depends on clinical status, not on fever alone.
  • Well, alert, drinking: oral antibiotics as outpatient
  • Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated, cannot take orally: admit for IV antibiotics
  • Always send urine culture before the first dose
  • Nitrite + leukocyte esterase positive = high probability of UTI
exam_pearl: Fever and chills alone do not mandate IV therapy; look for the words toxic, vomiting or not tolerating oral intake before choosing admission.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Pediatric with knee pain (single joint), limited range of motion, warmth, had gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago. US shows effusion. How to manage?
OptC: Synovial aspiration for analysis and culture
why_right: An acute single warm knee with limited range of motion and an effusion on US must be treated as possible septic arthritis until joint fluid proves otherwise. The preceding gastroenteritis suggests reactive arthritis, but that is a diagnosis of exclusion, so synovial aspiration with cell count, Gram stain and culture is the key step. Joint fluid examination both confirms or excludes infection and identifies the organism.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral ibuprofen: the treatment for reactive arthritis or transient synovitis once septic arthritis has been excluded. Starting it first risks missing a septic joint.
B. Oral aspirin / analgesia: aspirin is the classic treatment for rheumatic fever arthritis and is generally avoided in children otherwise (Reye syndrome). Analgesia alone does not address a possibly infected effusion.
D. IV antibiotics: right once septic arthritis is strongly suspected, but ideally after the joint is aspirated so culture is not sterilised. Here the question asks how to manage a new effusion, and aspiration comes first.
key_concept:
Acute monoarthritis with effusion = aspirate the joint.
  • Septic: fever, hot joint, refusal to move, very high synovial WBC with neutrophils, positive Gram stain or culture
  • Reactive: follows GI or GU infection by 1 to 4 weeks, sterile fluid, treated with NSAIDs
  • Transient synovitis: hip, post viral, well child, NSAIDs
  • Aspiration before antibiotics whenever possible
exam_pearl: A history of recent gastroenteritis tempts you toward reactive arthritis and NSAIDs, but a hot effusion is aspirated first because septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically.

stem: 7 yrs old girl with type 1 DM, recently with loss of weight, glucose 250 mg/dl. What is the best advice/approach for her?
OptA: Educate the family on how to use insulin
OptB: Give her pamphlet and for follow up
OptD: Postpone education till glucose is controlled
highlight_terms_source: 7 yrs old girl with type 1 DM
key_concept:
New or poorly controlled type 1 DM in a stable child: start insulin and educate the family.
  • DKA (hyperglycaemia + acidosis + ketosis): stabilise first with fluids and IV insulin
  • No DKA: subcutaneous insulin and structured family education
  • Teach injection technique, home glucose monitoring, sick day rules
  • Most important adverse effect to teach: hypoglycaemia
exam_pearl: Weight loss in type 1 DM signals insulin deficiency, which carbohydrate restriction cannot correct; the fork is DKA (stabilise first) versus stable (insulin with family education).
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 7-year-old child presents with upper abdominal pain that wakes him from sleep and subsides when eating. His mother mentions that he has a history of peptic ulcer previously. What is the most diagnostic for the suspected diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: upper abdominal pain that wakes him from sleep and subsides when eating
why_right: Epigastric pain that wakes him from sleep and is relieved by eating, in a child with a previous peptic ulcer, points to a duodenal ulcer, likely related to H. pylori. The lead in asks for the most diagnostic test, and upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsy is the gold standard: it shows the ulcer directly and the biopsy confirms H. pylori by histology, culture or rapid urease testing.
why_wrong_block:
B. Over-the-counter antacids: symptomatic treatment, not a diagnostic test; at best it would fit a mild dyspepsia question asking for initial symptom relief.
C. Give PPI: treatment of peptic ulcer disease once diagnosed (or empirical therapy in mild dyspepsia), but it diagnoses nothing and can mask H. pylori on later testing.
D. H. pylori antibiotic prophylaxis: there is no prophylactic regimen; eradication therapy is given only after H. pylori is confirmed.
key_concept:
Peptic ulcer disease: endoscopy is diagnostic, drugs are treatment.
  • Duodenal ulcer: pain relieved by food, nocturnal waking pain
  • Gastric ulcer: pain worse after food
  • Gold standard diagnosis: EGD with biopsy
  • Non invasive H. pylori tests: urea breath test, stool antigen
  • Confirmed H. pylori: triple therapy (PPI + two antibiotics)
exam_pearl: When the lead in is "most diagnostic", choose the test (EGD with biopsy), not a treatment option such as PPI or antacids.

stem: 5 years old girl came to emergency department complaining of fever, painful micturition. What is best management?
why_right: This recall's key is oral ampicillin: a 5 year old girl with painful micturition and fever who is not described as toxic or vomiting can be managed with an oral antibiotic. A closely matching question on uncomplicated cystitis in a 5 year old girl is keyed to oral amoxicillin (an aminopenicillin like ampicillin), which supports an oral aminopenicillin here.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral something: the recall does not name this drug. If it was an oral cephalosporin (cephalexin, cefixime) it would also be a reasonable oral choice; the source keyed ampicillin.
C. IV ciprofloxacin: fluoroquinolones are not first line in children because of cartilage toxicity concerns, and IV therapy is reserved for toxic children or those who cannot take oral medication.
D. IM ceftriaxone: used for children who are vomiting or too unwell for oral therapy, or as a single dose before oral step down; unnecessary for a child who can take oral antibiotics.
key_concept:
Childhood UTI: oral antibiotics unless the child is toxic or cannot tolerate oral intake.
  • Most common organism: E. coli
  • Well child: oral antibiotic after urine culture
  • Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated, young infant: IV or IM (e.g. ceftriaxone)
  • Avoid fluoroquinolones as first line in children
exam_pearl: In a well child, the route matters more than the drug name; reject IV and IM options unless the stem says toxic or vomiting.

stem: Child brought by his mother with lethargy, pallor, low grade subjective fever, lymphadenopathy for 2 months. What to do next?
why_right: Lethargy, pallor, low grade fever and lymphadenopathy for 2 months in a child raise concern for leukaemia. The lead in is what to do next and no labs have been done yet, so the first step is a CBC with peripheral blood film, which can show cytopenias and blasts. Bone marrow examination follows to confirm the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Virology screening: right when the picture suggests infectious mononucleosis or another viral cause (sore throat, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes on film). It does not address the malignancy red flags here and still needs a blood film first.
C. Bone marrow examination: the confirmatory test for leukaemia, done after the blood film is abnormal (blasts or cytopenias). It is not the first investigation when no blood count has been done.
key_concept:
Suspected childhood leukaemia: initial vs confirmatory test.
  • Next or initial step: CBC with peripheral blood film
  • Confirmatory: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
  • Red flags: persistent pallor and fatigue, unexplained fever, lymphadenopathy, bruising, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly
exam_pearl: Same stem, different lead in: "next" means blood film, "confirmatory" means bone marrow examination.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot note: No labs. A) blood film, confirmed by Hatim 100/120 in pediatric. Pallor + next (CBC not done, just pallor + lymphadenopathy, no thrombocytopenia) = blood film; initial to confirm / confirmatory = bone marrow.

stem: Child brought by his mother with lethargy, pallor, low grade subjective fever, lymphadenopathy for 2 months. What is the confirmatory test?
why_right: Lethargy, pallor, low grade fever and lymphadenopathy for 2 months in a child suggests leukaemia. The lead in asks for the confirmatory test, and bone marrow examination (aspiration and biopsy) is definitively diagnostic, establishing the blast percentage and lineage.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood film: the initial or next step, showing cytopenias or circulating blasts, but it cannot confirm leukaemia or classify it. It is the answer when the lead in asks what to do next.
B. Virology screening: right when a viral illness such as infectious mononucleosis is suspected; it does not confirm or exclude leukaemia.
key_concept:
Suspected childhood leukaemia: initial vs confirmatory test.
  • Initial: CBC with peripheral blood film
  • Confirmatory: bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
  • Bone marrow also allows immunophenotyping and cytogenetics
exam_pearl: "Confirmatory" in the lead in flips the answer from blood film to bone marrow examination.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Different recall from a friend exactly saying 'What is the confirmatory test?' Answer is C) bone marrow examination (confirmed).

stem: A child had chest pain, sore throat or some sort of infection, then he got pain in his right knee while left is perfect. How can you treat? There is redness and slight effusion on physical examination.
why_right: A child with a preceding sore throat who then develops a red knee with effusion (and possibly chest pain, suggesting carditis) fits post streptococcal disease, most likely acute rheumatic fever. The main symptomatic treatment of rheumatic fever arthritis and mild carditis is high dose oral acetylsalicylic acid, which gives a rapid response, so the source keys aspirin.
why_wrong_block:
B. Steroids: reserved for moderate to severe rheumatic carditis (e.g. heart failure); not the treatment for arthritis.
C. Reassurance: inappropriate because rheumatic fever needs anti-inflammatory treatment, eradication of group A strep with penicillin and secondary prophylaxis.
D. Other medication: unspecified in the recall; penicillin is also given to eradicate streptococci, but the symptomatic arthritis treatment asked for here is aspirin.
key_concept:
Acute rheumatic fever management.
  • Arthritis and mild carditis: high dose aspirin (or NSAID)
  • Moderate to severe carditis: add corticosteroids
  • Eradicate group A strep: penicillin
  • Secondary prophylaxis: long term benzathine penicillin
  • Diagnosis: Jones criteria with evidence of preceding strep infection
exam_pearl: Rheumatic arthritis is classically migratory polyarthritis with a dramatic response to aspirin; a single joint after sore throat may instead be post streptococcal reactive arthritis, which is treated with NSAIDs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller: 'My recall is bad on this one.' Pretty sure there was no investigation; chose ASA thinking it might be rheumatic fever related, however might be recall bias.

stem: 6 weeks presented w jaundice and alcoholic stool and he also has pulmonary stenosis, butterfly vertebrae and triangular face What is the possible diagnosis ?
why_right: Cholestatic jaundice with acholic (pale) stools at 6 weeks combined with pulmonary stenosis, butterfly vertebrae and a triangular face is the classic picture of Alagille syndrome. It is an autosomal dominant disorder (JAG1 or NOTCH2) with paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts, and the extrahepatic features distinguish it from biliary atresia.
why_wrong_block: A. Duodenal atresia: presents in the first days of life with bilious vomiting and a double bubble on X-ray, often with Down syndrome; it does not cause cholestatic jaundice with pale stools or butterfly vertebrae.
key_concept:
Neonatal cholestasis with pale stools: think biliary atresia vs Alagille syndrome.
  • Alagille: paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts + pulmonary stenosis + butterfly vertebrae + triangular face + posterior embryotoxon
  • Biliary atresia: isolated cholestasis with pale stools, needs urgent Kasai
  • Duodenal atresia: bilious vomiting, double bubble, Down syndrome
exam_pearl: Cholestasis with pale stools alone suggests biliary atresia; add a heart murmur (pulmonary stenosis) and butterfly vertebrae and it becomes Alagille syndrome.

stem: A newborn with Hemophilia A presents with bleeding. What is the appropriate treatment?
key_concept:
Haemophilia A bleeding: replace the missing factor.
  • Haemophilia A: factor VIII deficiency, prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets
  • Haemophilia B: factor IX deficiency, treat with factor IX
  • Inhibitors present: recombinant factor VIIa (bypassing agent)
  • Specific factor unavailable: cryoprecipitate or FFP
exam_pearl: Factor VII vs factor VIII is a classic recall slip; rFVIIa is only for haemophilia with inhibitors.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents to the clinic complaining of abdominal pain, frequent diarrhoea that is sometimes bloody, and pain usually accompanying defecation. His mother observed that he has lost weight over the last 3 months since the onset of the problem. The boy also has aches and pains of his joints. On examination, he looks ill, pale, with a so> abdomen, no tenderness or organomegaly (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: frequent diarrhoea that is sometimes bloody
aches and pains of his joints
why_right: A child with chronic diarrhea that is "sometimes bloody", pain accompanying defecation (rectal involvement, tenesmus/urgency), weight loss over 3 months, pallor and joint aches has inflammatory bowel disease. Visible blood in the stool tips the choice to ulcerative colitis, a continuous mucosal colitis starting at the rectum. Arthralgia is a common extraintestinal manifestation of IBD, and anemia with low albumin reflects chronic inflammation and blood/protein loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Celiac disease gives non-bloody malabsorptive diarrhea, distension and poor growth; it does not explain bloody stools with painful defecation and arthralgia.
B. Crohn's disease also causes weight loss, anemia and arthralgia, but stools are usually non-bloody with periumbilical/RLQ pain, oral ulcers or perianal disease; with frank bloody diarrhea, choose UC.
D. Chronic dysentery (e.g. amoebic or persistent bacterial) can give prolonged bloody diarrhea, but stool microscopy/culture would show the organism and it does not explain arthralgia as an extraintestinal feature; this cluster in a child is IBD.
key_concept:
Chronic diarrhea + weight loss + extraintestinal signs in a child = IBD; blood decides the type.
  • UC: bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, rectum upward, continuous
  • Crohn's: non-bloody, RLQ pain/mass, oral ulcers, perianal fistula, skip lesions
  • Extraintestinal: arthritis/arthralgia, erythema nodosum, uveitis, growth failure
  • Labs: anemia, low albumin, raised CRP/ESR
  • Confirm: ileocolonoscopy with biopsy
exam_pearl: Bloody diarrhea with IBD features: pick UC over Crohn's; if UC is not listed, Crohn's becomes the answer.

stem: 12 years old presented with fever and night sweat and painless cervical lymph nodes enlargment FNA: show Reed–Sternberg cells What the diagnosis?
why_right: Reed–Sternberg cells on cytology are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma. The picture fits: an older child/adolescent with painless cervical lymphadenopathy plus B symptoms (fever, night sweats). Note that FNA is suggestive only; definitive diagnosis and subtyping require excisional lymph node biopsy.
why_wrong_block: A. AML presents with marrow failure (pallor, bleeding, infections), blasts on the blood film and sometimes gum infiltration; it does not show Reed–Sternberg cells in a lymph node.
key_concept:
Painless cervical nodes + B symptoms in a teen = think lymphoma; Reed–Sternberg cell = Hodgkin.
  • B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss
  • Hodgkin: contiguous nodal spread, often mediastinal mass, bimodal age
  • Non-Hodgkin (e.g. Burkitt, lymphoblastic): rapid growth, extranodal, abdominal or mediastinal mass
  • Diagnosis: excisional node biopsy (FNA is not enough)
  • Alternatives to exclude: reactive nodes, TB lymphadenitis
exam_pearl: Reed–Sternberg (owl's eye) cell = Hodgkin; a node that is painful with alcohol is a classic Hodgkin clue.

stem: 3 day age neonate c/s delivery have desaturation and grunting also blue lips around mouth
key_concept:
Newborn respiratory distress: decide by gestation, onset and CXR.
  • TTN: term CS, onset within hours, fissural fluid, settles by 2 to 3 days
  • RDS: preterm, onset at birth, ground glass + air bronchograms, low volumes
  • Pneumonia/sepsis: risk factors, any time, patchy infiltrates
  • Meconium aspiration: post term, stained liquor, hyperinflation with patchy opacities
exam_pearl: CS + term + early onset = TTN; if the baby is preterm think RDS, if distress appears or persists beyond the first days think infection.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 3 (weeks old or days old baby) presented to the ER with lethargy poor feeding, hypotonia, irritability (i think), his bedside glucose was 35 mg/dl. Critical labs was drown before glucose correction. Lab results: beta-hydroxybutyrate levels 0.1 (Normal >1.5) Glucose 2.2 mmol/l (low) Fasting insulin 44 (i think normal) Cortisol 4 hours above normal (i think slightly high) Other labs normal
why_right: The critical sample shows hypoglycemia with low beta-hydroxybutyrate (0.1), meaning hypoketotic hypoglycemia, together with an insulin level that is detectable/high while glucose is low. Insulin should be suppressed during hypoglycemia, so inappropriate insulin plus suppressed ketones (insulin blocks lipolysis and ketogenesis) defines hyperinsulinism. In a neonate with lethargy, poor feeding and hypotonia this is congenital hyperinsulinism.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adrenal insufficiency causes ketotic hypoglycemia with low cortisol (often hyponatremia and hyperkalemia); here cortisol is not low and ketones are suppressed.
B. Glycogen storage disease type I gives fasting hypoglycemia with hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis and hyperlipidemia, with insulin appropriately suppressed.
D. Growth hormone deficiency (often as hypopituitarism with cortisol deficiency) causes hypoglycemia with appropriately suppressed insulin; neonatal clues are microphallus, midline defects and prolonged jaundice, none given here.
key_concept:
Read the critical sample: ketones + insulin sort neonatal hypoglycemia.
  • Low ketones + inappropriately high insulin: hyperinsulinism
  • Low ketones + low insulin: fatty acid oxidation defect
  • Suppressed insulin + low cortisol/GH: adrenal or pituitary deficiency
  • Hepatomegaly + lactic acidosis: glycogen storage disease I
  • Hyperinsulinism also: high glucose need, glucagon response
exam_pearl: Any measurable insulin during hypoglycemia is inappropriate; hypoketotic + insulin present = hyperinsulinism.

stem: A 12 years old female (I think) had a loss of consciousness after sitting in the sun for sometime. what is the red flag for this patient?
OptD: Family history of early unexplained death
highlight_terms_source: loss of consciousness after sitting in the sun
why_right: Syncope after sitting in the sun (heat, prolonged posture) is usually vasovagal (reflex) syncope and benign. The red flag that suggests a cardiac cause is a family history of early unexplained (sudden) death, which raises inherited arrhythmia syndromes (long QT, Brugada) or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mandates ECG and cardiac evaluation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Brief jerky movements commonly occur during vasovagal syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion (convulsive syncope) and are not by themselves a red flag.
B. Dizziness, lightheadedness or blurred vision before LOC is a typical vasovagal prodrome and is reassuring.
C. Option not recalled; judge any remaining choice against the cardiac red flag list below.
key_concept:
Syncope red flags point to a cardiac cause.
  • Family history of sudden or unexplained death at a young age
  • Syncope during exertion or while supine
  • Preceded by palpitations or chest pain, no prodrome
  • Triggered by loud noise, fright or swimming (long QT)
  • Abnormal ECG or murmur
  • Benign: prodrome, prolonged standing, heat, quick recovery
exam_pearl: Prodrome and heat point to vasovagal; family sudden death, exertion or no warning means ECG and cardiology.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option C not recalled (printed as a stray 'C' after option B).

stem: 7 month child with asthma symptoms what is the diagnostic test
key_concept:
Under 5 years asthma is diagnosed clinically.
  • Recurrent wheeze/cough, triggers, atopy or family history
  • Response to bronchodilator or controller trial
  • Infant wheeze: consider bronchiolitis, foreign body, reflux, CF, malformations
  • Spirometry from about 5 to 6 years
exam_pearl: If the answer list has 'history, exam and response to bronchodilator', that wins in a young child; spirometry only for school age.

stem: A boy presented with polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturia Urine osmolality 120 Serum osmolality 300 (Numbers are not accurate) Water deprivation test: After giving desmopressin urine osmolality improved. What is the best long-term management?
highlight_terms_source: After giving desmopressin urine osmolality improved
why_right: Polyuria and polydipsia with dilute urine (low urine osmolality) and high serum osmolality is diabetes insipidus. The urine fails to concentrate with water deprivation but concentrates after desmopressin, proving the kidney responds to ADH, so the defect is ADH deficiency (central DI). Long-term treatment is replacement with desmopressin.
why_wrong_block: A. Fluid restriction is dangerous in DI (worsens dehydration and hypernatremia); it is the treatment of SIADH, and water restriction is only used diagnostically under supervision.
key_concept:
Water deprivation then desmopressin separates the polyurias.
  • Concentrates with deprivation: primary polydipsia
  • No rise with deprivation, rises with desmopressin: central DI, treat with desmopressin
  • No rise with either: nephrogenic DI, treat with thiazide + low salt diet (stop the offending drug)
  • Causes of central DI: head trauma, surgery, craniopharyngioma, LCH
exam_pearl: Response to desmopressin = central DI; no response = nephrogenic DI, where thiazides are used.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed version: pediatric with polydipsia, polyuria, urine osmolality 150, serum osmolality 350; no change after fluid deprivation but osmolality increased with vasopressin; long-term medication? Options: Desmopressin (DDAVP) [highlighted]; i forgot but i think steroids?

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever
key_concept:
Chronic bloody diarrhea + weight loss + fever in a child = suspect IBD.
  • Exclude infection: stool cultures, C. difficile
  • Bloods: CBC, CRP/ESR, albumin; fecal calprotectin
  • Diagnostic: ileocolonoscopy with biopsies (+ upper endoscopy in children)
  • Severe or toxic: admit, IV fluids, IV steroids
exam_pearl: Red flags (blood, weight loss, fever) mean investigate, not treat symptomatically; acid suppression is never the answer for bloody diarrhea.

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: chronic diarrhea, blood in stool, weight loss, and fever
key_concept:
Suspected pediatric IBD: stable = endoscopy with biopsy; toxic = admit.
  • First exclude infection: stool cultures, C. difficile
  • CBC, CRP/ESR, albumin, fecal calprotectin
  • Ileocolonoscopy + upper endoscopy with biopsies confirm
  • MR enterography for small bowel extent
  • CT only for acute complications
exam_pearl: Diagnosis of IBD rests on endoscopy with biopsy; CT and PPI are traps, and 'admit' wins when the child is toxic.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the Primary Clinic because her mother noticed she is pale. She has a history of drinking cow’s milk and biscuit daily and didn’t eat red meat low hbg low mcv low ferritin A slight increase in reticulocyte count around 1.8 and normal was 1.2 What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: low hbg low mcv low ferritin
key_concept:
Low ferritin is the decisive test for iron deficiency.
  • Toddler + excess cow's milk + no meat = iron deficiency
  • Cow's milk: iron poor, displaces solids, occult GI loss
  • Thal trait: microcytosis, normal ferritin, high RBC count
  • Chronic disease: ferritin normal/high
  • Spherocytosis: hemolysis, high retics, spherocytes
exam_pearl: Ferritin decides: low ferritin = iron deficiency; normal or high ferritin with microcytosis points to thalassemia trait or chronic disease.

stem: 6 months old infant brought to vaccination clinic He had huge swelling at injection site when previous DTaP given Now he have URTI with temperature 37.9 What to do regarding Dtap vaccine ?
highlight_terms_source: huge swelling at injection site when previous DTaP
why_right: Give the DTaP dose now. A "huge swelling at injection site" after the previous dose is a local reaction, which is not a contraindication to further DTaP doses, and a mild URTI with a temperature of 37.9 is a minor illness that should not delay vaccination. Deferring for trivial reasons only leaves the infant unprotected against pertussis at the age it is most dangerous.
why_wrong_block:
B. There is no required waiting interval after a local reaction; delaying 2 months leaves the infant unprotected and off schedule for no benefit.
C. Only a moderate or severe acute illness justifies postponing a vaccine; a mild URTI with low grade temperature does not, so waiting for it to resolve is a missed opportunity.
D. Dropping the pertussis component (DT) is reserved for true pertussis contraindications such as encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose; a local swelling is not one of them.
key_concept:
Local reactions and minor illness are NOT reasons to withhold or delay DTaP.
  • Redness, swelling (even large), low or moderate fever after a dose: reassure and continue schedule
  • Mild illness (URTI, low grade fever): vaccinate now
  • Moderate or severe acute illness: postpone until improved
  • Encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis dose: contraindication, give DT
  • Progressive or unstable neurological disorder: withhold until stabilized
  • Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component: contraindication
exam_pearl: Large local swelling plus a sniffle is still a 'vaccinate today' case; only encephalopathy or anaphylaxis changes the DTaP plan.

stem: 6 or 4 years old child with DM type 1 complaining of repeated hypoglycemia at night, his current medication's are rapid acting insulin before meal and basal insulin at night what is the most appropriate modification on his current regimen:
OptB: decrease the dose of basal insulin
why_right: The hypoglycemia is "at night" and the only insulin acting overnight is the "basal insulin at night", so the basal dose is too high and should be reduced. Matching the adjustment to the timing of the low is the rule: fasting or nocturnal lows point to basal insulin, lows after meals point to prandial insulin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waking a young child for a 3 AM meal treats the symptom, not the cause, and is impractical; the fix is to lower the excess basal insulin.
C. Rapid acting insulin before meals causes lows in the hours after meals; it would be reduced if the hypoglycemia were postprandial, not nocturnal.
D. Feeding extra carbohydrate to cover too much insulin leads to weight gain and erratic control; it does not correct the overdosed basal insulin.
key_concept:
Adjust the insulin that is acting when the low occurs.
  • Nocturnal or fasting hypoglycemia: reduce basal (long acting) insulin
  • Postprandial hypoglycemia: reduce the prandial (rapid acting) dose before that meal
  • Both: reduce both
  • Exercise related lows: reduce the pre exercise prandial dose
  • Never stop basal insulin in type 1 DM (risk of DKA)
  • New recurrent lows soon after diagnosis: think honeymoon period
exam_pearl: Timing decides the insulin: night lows = basal, after meal lows = bolus.

stem: child presented with short stature, mild jaundice and he is pale with frontal bossing and maxillary and hepatosplenomegaly and lossing weight What is the important investigating to short stature ?
highlight_terms_source: pale with frontal bossing and maxillary
why_right: The clues pale, mild jaundice, frontal bossing, maxillary prominence and hepatosplenomegaly describe chronic hemolytic anemia with extramedullary erythropoiesis, classically beta thalassemia major. Here the short stature and weight loss are secondary to the anemia, so the key first investigation is the hemoglobin (CBC), followed by indices and hemoglobin electrophoresis to confirm the type.
why_wrong_block:
A. The jaundice here is hemolytic (unconjugated) and the organomegaly is from extramedullary hematopoiesis, so LFTs do not identify the cause; they matter later for iron overload liver damage.
C. TSH is part of the work up of unexplained short stature (hypothyroid child: short, overweight, delayed bone age), but this child has a clear hemolytic picture that explains the growth failure.
D. Pituitary (growth hormone) testing fits a short child with low IGF-1, delayed bone age and otherwise normal exam, not one with pallor, jaundice and skeletal marrow expansion.
key_concept:
Short stature with pallor, jaundice, frontal bossing and hepatosplenomegaly = chronic hemolytic anemia (beta thalassemia major).
  • First test: hemoglobin / CBC (severe microcytic anemia)
  • Then reticulocytes, blood film and hemoglobin electrophoresis (raised HbF and HbA2)
  • Frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth (chipmunk face): marrow expansion
  • Hepatosplenomegaly: extramedullary erythropoiesis
  • Endocrine causes (TSH, GH) are tested when there is no systemic clue
exam_pearl: When a short child has a systemic disease picture, test the disease (Hb here), not the growth hormones.

stem: 10 years old come to your clinic with dental caries, high consumption of chocolate and sugar, and low vegetables and fruit intake, what is the prevention point of counselling?
highlight_terms_source: high consumption of chocolate and sugar
why_right: The child's caries are driven by his diet: "high consumption of chocolate and sugar" with "low vegetables and fruit". The prevention point is therefore dietary counselling: cutting the amount and especially the frequency of sugary snacks and drinks and building a balanced diet, which addresses the cause rather than one adjunct.
why_wrong_block:
B. Caries is caused by free sugars and how often they are eaten, not carbohydrate in general; a blanket 'eat less carb' message is too narrow and misses the fruit and vegetable deficit.
C. Fluoride is a useful adjunct to strengthen enamel, but it does not remove the cause; the main counselling point when diet is clearly the problem is dietary change.
key_concept:
Caries prevention in children starts with the cause.
  • Diet: reduce frequency and amount of free sugars, sweets and sugary drinks
  • Oral hygiene: twice daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste
  • Fluoride supplements, varnish or mouthwash: adjuncts per dentist and age
  • Toddlers: no bottle in bed (nursing bottle caries)
  • Regular dental visits
exam_pearl: When the stem spells out a bad diet, the counselling answer is diet, not a fluoride product.

stem: A 34-week preterm infant was delivered using vacuum extraction (ventouse). On day 2 of life, the baby appears pale and lethargic. On physical examination, there is a fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and is increasing in size. Laboratory investigations show: Hemoglobin: Low, Platelets: Normal, PT: Normal, PTT: Normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines
why_right: After a vacuum (ventouse) delivery, a fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and is increasing in size with a baby who is pale and lethargic and has low hemoglobin is a subgaleal hemorrhage. The subgaleal space can hold a large part of a neonate's blood volume, so this is hypovolemic shock: the next step is resuscitation with volume and packed RBC transfusion. Normal platelets, PT and PTT mean the bleed is mechanical, not a coagulopathy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation fits caput succedaneum (soft, crosses sutures, maximal at birth and shrinking) or cephalohematoma (limited by sutures, stable baby); a growing swelling with pallor, lethargy and low Hb is life threatening.
B. IV antibiotics would be for sepsis or an infected cephalohematoma (fever, erythema); here the picture is acute blood loss, not infection.
C. The option text was not recalled; whatever it was (e.g. vitamin K or plasma), it cannot outrank volume and blood replacement in a shocked, anemic baby with normal coagulation.
key_concept:
Neonatal scalp swellings after delivery:
  • Caput succedaneum: soft edema, crosses sutures, largest at birth, resolves in days: reassure
  • Cephalohematoma: subperiosteal, does NOT cross sutures, firm edge, may cause jaundice: observe
  • Subgaleal hemorrhage: fluctuant, crosses sutures, expands after birth, pallor, tachycardia, shock, falling Hb: emergency
  • Subgaleal: classic after vacuum extraction
  • Management: volume and packed RBCs, monitor head circumference and Hb, correct any coagulopathy
exam_pearl: Crosses sutures plus enlarging plus pale baby = subgaleal hemorrhage, not caput; transfuse, do not observe.

stem: 7y present to the ER c/o 5 day hx of SOB with white sputum which get yellow after a while, was dx with pneumonia which was treated with ABx and get better. 2 days after, start to have SOB and his symptoms get worse, 85% on RA. Vitals BP 90/70 HR 123 Temp 37. VBG PCO2 70 PO2 45 pH 7.2 (or 7.1, the unit was not the usual unit of pH). What is the most likely cause of his presentation?
why_right: The gas shows PCO2 70 with pH 7.2 (acute respiratory acidosis) and the child is hypoxic at 85% on room air, tachycardic (HR 123) with a narrow pulse pressure. Failure of both oxygenation and ventilation after worsening pneumonia is acute respiratory failure (hypercapnic, type 2, with hypoxemia), which is the diagnosis that explains the whole picture and dictates urgent ventilatory support.
why_wrong_block:
A. 'Complication of pneumonia' is too vague to be the answer; the gas pins down the specific complication, which is failure of gas exchange.
B. ARDS needs bilateral opacities on imaging and a low PaO2/FiO2 ratio with PEEP, and early ARDS usually gives hypoxemia with low or normal CO2; neither imaging nor these criteria are provided here, while the marked CO2 retention fits respiratory failure.
D. A parapneumonic effusion would be suggested by dullness, reduced breath sounds and a fluid level on X-ray; it does not by itself explain a PCO2 of 70 with acidosis.
key_concept:
Read the gas to classify respiratory failure.
  • Type 1 (hypoxemic): low PaO2, normal or low PaCO2 (pneumonia, aspiration, early ARDS)
  • Type 2 (hypercapnic): high PaCO2 with acidosis (fatigue, airway or neuromuscular failure)
  • Acute type 2: pH falls with rising CO2
  • On a VBG, judge oxygenation by SpO2, not venous PO2
  • ARDS: Berlin criteria (timing within 1 week, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 on PEEP, not cardiac)
exam_pearl: High CO2 with acidosis in a tiring child = respiratory failure; ARDS needs bilateral infiltrates you were not shown.

stem: 28 weeks neonate developed desaturation and bradycardia improving with stimulation. What's the underlying cause?
highlight_terms_source: desaturation and bradycardia improving with stimulation
why_right: A 28 week neonate with episodes of desaturation and bradycardia that improve with stimulation has apnea of prematurity. Its cause is the immature brainstem (central) control of breathing, which is why it is inversely related to gestational age, responds to tactile stimulation and is treated with caffeine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypoglycemia can trigger apnea and must be excluded, but it is a secondary cause shown by a low glucose; the stem gives a typical premature infant with no metabolic clue.
B. Meconium aspiration affects term or post term babies born through meconium stained liquor and causes persistent respiratory distress, not intermittent self limiting spells in a 28 week infant.
C. Airway malformations give obstructive symptoms (stridor, distress, feeding difficulty) that do not resolve with simple stimulation.
key_concept:
Apnea of prematurity: central immaturity of respiratory control.
  • Pause of 20 seconds or more, or shorter with bradycardia or desaturation
  • More frequent the more premature the baby
  • Responds to stimulation
  • Exclude secondary causes: sepsis, hypoglycemia, anemia, IVH, temperature instability
  • Treatment: stimulation, caffeine, CPAP if persistent
  • Resolves as the infant matures
exam_pearl: Preterm spells that stop with a flick of the foot = apnea of prematurity (central), treat with caffeine.

stem: Pediatric (not sure about the age) patient with clear case of brucellosis. Hx of drink raw milk from goat, patient had pain in the knee. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
key_concept:
Brucellosis treatment is combination therapy for weeks.
  • Age 8 years or older and adults: doxycycline plus rifampicin (or streptomycin) for 6 weeks
  • Younger than 8 years: TMP-SMX plus rifampicin
  • Spondylitis or sacroiliitis: extend to about 12 weeks
  • Neurobrucellosis: months of therapy
  • Pregnancy: avoid doxycycline
  • Monotherapy: high relapse
exam_pearl: In pediatric brucellosis, the child's age (8 years) decides doxycycline vs TMP-SMX.

Compiler note: Compiler note: Age > 8 years: Doxycycline; Age < 8 years: TMP SMX. (Age not recalled, so no option marked.)

stem: A 13 year old boy has arthritis and when he exercises he has joint pain and chest pain. He started to take penicillin G monthly. When will he stop taking penicillin?
why_right: A 13 year old with arthritis plus chest pain on exertion is being treated as rheumatic fever with carditis. With carditis, secondary prophylaxis continues for 10 years after the last attack or until age 21, whichever is longer: 13 + 10 = age 23, which is longer than age 21.
why_wrong_block:
A. 2 years is shorter than any recommended duration of secondary prophylaxis after rheumatic fever.
B. 5 years after the attack (age 18) is the rule only for rheumatic fever without carditis, and even then it continues until 21 if that is longer.
D. Until age 21 is the answer for rheumatic fever without carditis in this age group (5 years or to 21, whichever longer); carditis extends it to 10 years.
key_concept:
Secondary prophylaxis: whichever is LONGER of years since last attack or the age limit.
  • No carditis: 5 years or until age 21
  • Carditis, no residual valve disease: 10 years or until age 21
  • Carditis with residual valve disease: 10 years or until age 40 (lifelong may be needed)
  • Drug: monthly IM benzathine penicillin
  • Do the arithmetic: age at attack plus years, then compare with the age limit
exam_pearl: Chest pain or carditis in the stem switches 5 years to 10 years; add it to the current age before comparing with 21.

stem: Scenario about baby with bronchiolitis symptoms, imaging of choice:
why_right: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in an infant with URTI symptoms followed by wheeze, crackles and tachypnea. When imaging is asked for, the chest X ray is the modality of choice: it shows hyperinflation (air trapping), peribronchial thickening and patchy atelectasis, and it is the test used if pneumonia or a foreign body needs excluding.
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: no role in acute lower respiratory infection in an infant; slow, needs sedation, and adds nothing to management.
C. Ultrasound: lung ultrasound is a research or point of care tool, not the standard imaging for bronchiolitis; ultrasound is first line for things like intussusception or pyloric stenosis.
D. CT: high radiation and not indicated; reserved for complications or suspected structural lung disease, not a routine viral bronchiolitis.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = clinical diagnosis; imaging only if needed, and then CXR.
  • Cause: RSV most common
  • Picture: infant, coryza then wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, retractions
  • CXR (if done): hyperinflation, peribronchial cuffing, patchy atelectasis
  • CXR not routine; do it if pneumonia or foreign body suspected
  • Organism: nasopharyngeal aspirate
  • Treatment: supportive (oxygen, hydration)
exam_pearl: If the question asks whether imaging is routinely needed, the answer is no; if it asks which imaging, it is the chest X ray.

stem: TTN imaging feature?
why_right: Transient tachypnea of the newborn is caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, classically after a cesarean section at term. That retained fluid shows on chest X ray as fluid in the fissures (especially the horizontal fissure) with perihilar linear streaks and mild hyperinflation.
why_wrong_block: B. Basal infiltration: suggests pneumonia or aspiration (for example meconium aspiration gives patchy coarse infiltrates); it is not the TTN pattern.
key_concept:
Neonatal CXR patterns:
  • TTN: fluid in fissures, perihilar streaks, term CS baby, self resolving
  • RDS: diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular) with air bronchograms, preterm, surfactant deficiency
  • Meconium aspiration: patchy coarse infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • Pneumonia: focal or patchy consolidation
exam_pearl: Term + cesarean + fluid in the horizontal fissure = TTN; preterm + ground glass = RDS.

stem: 9 y/o boy with hx of URTI came with neck tenderness, his labs: Low TSH, Low T4, high ESR/CRP I think. Diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clues are a recent URTI, neck tenderness and a high ESR/CRP with a suppressed TSH: this is subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, a painful post viral thyroiditis. Inflammation releases stored hormone, so TSH falls; later the gland can pass through a hypothyroid phase before recovering.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves disease: low TSH with high T4, but the gland is non tender, ESR is normal, and there may be eye signs or diffuse uptake; it does not follow a URTI with neck pain.
C. Hashimoto thyroiditis: painless goiter with high TSH (hypothyroidism) and positive anti TPO antibodies; inflammatory markers are not raised.
D. Euthyroid sick syndrome: abnormal TFTs (low T3 first, sometimes low T4 and TSH) in a child who is acutely, seriously ill, such as in ICU; it causes no neck tenderness or raised ESR.
key_concept:
Painful thyroid + recent URTI + high ESR = subacute thyroiditis.
  • Labs: low TSH, high T4/T3 in the thyrotoxic phase, high ESR/CRP
  • Radioactive iodine uptake: low (distinguishes from Graves)
  • Course: thyrotoxic, then possible hypothyroid phase, then recovery
  • Treatment: NSAIDs or steroids for pain, beta blocker for symptoms
  • Graves: diffuse high uptake, non tender
exam_pearl: Tenderness and high ESR beat the exact hormone numbers: a tender gland after a viral illness is subacute thyroiditis even if the recalled T4 looks off.

stem: A father comes with his 3 years old daughter that missed (MMR, OPV, PCV, measles) due to travel and sickness. What to do at this visit? (Options exactly as in the exam, same order.)
OptA: Give polio vaccine only at this visit
OptB: start a catch up plan for vaccination
why_right: A child who has missed several vaccines should be brought up to date with a catch up schedule starting at this visit: give all due vaccines that can be given together and book the rest at the minimum intervals. The series is never restarted, travel or past illness is not a contraindication, and delay only prolongs the period of vulnerability.
why_wrong_block:
A. Give polio vaccine only: needlessly delays protection; multiple vaccines (including live MMR) can be given at the same visit, so MMR and PCV should not be held back.
C. Wait until school age: leaves a 3 year old unprotected against measles and pneumococcus for years; catch up starts now, not at school entry.
D. Vaccinations are useless nowadays: false and unprofessional; outbreaks of measles occur when coverage drops.
key_concept:
Missed vaccines = catch up now, do not restart.
  • Give all due vaccines at the same visit if possible
  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella): same day or at least 4 weeks apart
  • MMR minimum age 12 months; dose 2 at least 4 weeks after dose 1
  • PCV and Hib not needed in healthy children 5 years or older
  • Minor illness and travel are not contraindications
exam_pearl: Any option that restarts the series, delays, or gives only one vaccine is wrong; the answer is catch up starting today.

stem: 6 Y/O boy brought by his mother c/o fatigue and O/E hepatosplenomegaly, labs showed WBC 2.5 Hb 8 also plt low. What is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: A 6 year old with fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly and low WBC, Hb and platelets has pancytopenia with organomegaly, which points to marrow infiltration such as leukemia. The lead in is confirm the diagnosis, and only bone marrow examination (aspirate and biopsy) establishes it and classifies the disease.
why_wrong_block: B. Blood film: a quick supportive step that may show blasts, but it cannot confirm or classify leukemia and may be blast free (aleukemic); it would be the answer if the question asked for the initial test.
key_concept:
Two or more cell lines down = bone marrow.
  • Pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly or lymph nodes: think leukemia, confirm by bone marrow
  • Pancytopenia without organomegaly: think aplastic anemia, also bone marrow
  • Isolated low platelets after viral illness: ITP, marrow not needed (increased megakaryocytes if done)
exam_pearl: Initial test = CBC and film; confirmatory test = bone marrow examination.

Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0704B).

stem: A full term baby after CS developed tachypnea and low oxygen saturation, chest x-ray is shown, what is the diagnosis?
why_right: A full term baby born by cesarean section who develops tachypnea and mild desaturation soon after birth has transient tachypnea of the newborn. Without labor, fetal lung fluid is cleared slowly; the chest X ray shows fluid in the fissures and perihilar streaks, and it resolves with supportive care within days.
why_wrong_block: A. Diaphragmatic hernia: bowel loops in the chest with mediastinal shift, a scaphoid abdomen and absent breath sounds on one side, often known antenatally; it gives severe distress from birth, not a CS related wet lung.
key_concept:
Neonatal tachypnea by context:
  • Term + CS + fluid in fissures: TTN, self resolving
  • Preterm + ground glass, air bronchograms: RDS
  • Meconium stained liquor + patchy infiltrates: meconium aspiration
  • Scaphoid abdomen + bowel loops in chest: diaphragmatic hernia, insert NG tube, avoid bag mask
exam_pearl: Cesarean at term is the TTN keyword; prematurity flips it to RDS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall screenshots only. Another version on the same card: 'Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?' (CXR shown) with option A. Transient tachypnea of newborn (bold), and a handwritten note 'Q Egg shape'. Reference image: radiological findings in TTN (fluid in the horizontal fissure).

stem: Meningitis case about child who got all signs of meningitis, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness after URTI. What would you see in lumbar puncture? (100% this is almost all information you can get from the Qs)
OptA: Elevated leukocytes predominant neutrophils high protein, low glucose
OptB: Elevated leukocytes predominant lymphocytes normal protein, normal glucose
OptD: Elevated leukocytes predominant lymphocytes high protein, low glucose
why_right: This recall's key is viral meningitis: meningism appearing after a URTI in a child is read as a viral (for example enteroviral) meningitis, and viral CSF shows a raised white count with lymphocyte predominance, normal protein and normal glucose. Normal glucose is the single most useful feature separating viral from bacterial and TB meningitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neutrophils, high protein, low glucose: bacterial meningitis; it would be the answer with a toxic child, purpura, turbid CSF or organisms on Gram stain.
C. Normal leukocytes: makes meningitis unlikely; a child with neck stiffness, photophobia and altered consciousness is expected to have pleocytosis (a normal count with meningism suggests meningismus or very early disease).
D. Lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose: tuberculous (or fungal) meningitis, with a subacute course over weeks, TB exposure and cranial nerve palsies.
key_concept:
CSF by cause:
  • Bacterial: neutrophils, high protein, low glucose, turbid
  • Viral: lymphocytes, normal or mildly high protein, normal glucose
  • TB: lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose, subacute course
  • Glucose is the key fork: normal = viral
exam_pearl: Lymphocytes alone do not make it viral; lymphocytes with low glucose is TB.

stem: Child with wide complex tachy. Gave BP but I can't recall number but was low.
why_right: A wide complex tachycardia with low BP is unstable (presumed VT with a pulse), and any unstable tachyarrhythmia is treated with immediate synchronized cardioversion, with sedation if it does not delay the shock. Drugs are only for the stable patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adenosine: for stable regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT) after vagal maneuvers; it may be considered in stable regular monomorphic wide complex tachycardia, never as treatment of an unstable one.
B. Amiodarone: the drug for stable wide complex tachycardia or after cardioversion; giving it to a hypotensive child delays definitive treatment.
key_concept:
Tachycardia with a pulse:
  • Unstable (hypotension, shock, altered consciousness, heart failure): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable narrow, regular: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine
  • Stable wide: amiodarone or procainamide, expert advice; adenosine only if regular and monomorphic
  • Pulseless VT: defibrillation (unsynchronized), not cardioversion
exam_pearl: Check stability first; low BP makes the answer cardioversion regardless of QRS width.

stem: Pedo patient presented with abdominal pain and bloody stool what is the most likely cause
why_right: Bloody stool with abdominal pain means an invasive (inflammatory) colitis. Among the options only Campylobacter jejuni invades the mucosa and causes bloody diarrhea; it is one of the commonest bacterial causes of dysentery in children, often from undercooked poultry, and is treated with azithromycin when therapy is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rotavirus: commonest cause of severe watery diarrhea with vomiting and dehydration in infants; stool is not bloody.
B. Norovirus: outbreaks of acute vomiting and watery diarrhea (schools, cruises); non bloody and short lived.
C. Cryptosporidium: watery, often prolonged diarrhea, especially from swimming pools or in immunocompromised patients; not bloody.
key_concept:
Bloody diarrhea = invasive organism.

stem: A Child with Kawasaki disease, already received IVIG and IV aspirin, his symptoms are still not improving, what will you do next?

  • Carditis/coronary change: infliximab, then tapering oral prednisolone, then pulse IV methylprednisolone
  • Second IVIG is not first line once carditis is present
  • Echocardiography assesses the coronaries
  • Poor IVIG response predictors: high CRP, neutrophilia, low albumin, low sodium, high liver enzymes, age under 12 months

stem: Child diagnosed with kawasaki disease, started on High dose Aspirin and IVIG, after 3 days, child was not responding, there was left coronary artery dilation. What is most appropriate treatment in this case?
why_right: The child is IVIG-refractory ("not responding" after high dose aspirin and IVIG) and already has coronary involvement ("left coronary artery dilation"). In that branch a second IVIG is not first line and rescue anti-inflammatory therapy is needed; among the options, IV methylprednisolone is the only rescue agent, so it is the key.
why_wrong_block:
B. Low dose aspirin is the antiplatelet maintenance phase once fever has settled (continued until coronaries are normal on echo); it does nothing to control ongoing vasculitis in a non-responder.
C. Oral oseltamivir treats influenza; it matters in Kawasaki only because influenza or varicella on aspirin carries Reye syndrome risk, not as treatment of refractory disease.
key_concept:
Refractory Kawasaki: decide by carditis.
  • No carditis: second IVIG first
  • Carditis or coronary dilation: infliximab, tapering oral prednisolone, pulse IV methylprednisolone
  • Aspirin: high dose in acute phase, low dose antiplatelet afterwards
  • Echo is the test to follow the coronaries
exam_pearl: If infliximab were listed it would compete with steroids in the carditis branch; with only these options, the steroid is the rescue.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 1419. Refractory Kawasaki with carditis present: infliximab, taper oral prednisolone, pulse IV methylprednisolone (second dose IVIG not first line when carditis present).

stem: A 4-year-old boy is diagnosed with Kawasaki Disease on day 8 of illness. He is admitted to the hospital for further management. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment regimen?
highlight_terms_source: Kawasaki Disease on day 8 of illness
why_right: This is a newly diagnosed Kawasaki disease ("day 8 of illness", asking for the initial regimen). Standard initial therapy is a single high dose IVIG infusion plus aspirin, ideally within the first 10 days of illness to reduce coronary aneurysm risk, so day 8 is still the ideal window.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aspirin with IV corticosteroid: steroids are an adjunct only in selected high-risk patients or a rescue for IVIG failure; they do not replace IVIG as initial therapy.
C. IVIG with cyclosporine: cyclosporine is a later-line option for disease refractory to IVIG and other rescues, not part of the first regimen.
D. Aspirin with infliximab: infliximab is a rescue for IVIG-refractory disease (especially with carditis), not the initial treatment.
key_concept:
Kawasaki initial treatment = IVIG plus aspirin.
  • Best given within 10 days of fever onset; still give after day 10 if fever or inflammation persists
  • Echocardiography at diagnosis and on follow-up
  • Refractory: second IVIG (no carditis) or infliximab/steroids
  • Cyclosporine: later rescue only
exam_pearl: "Initial" regimen always contains IVIG; any option with a biologic or immunosuppressant is a rescue line.

stem: Child 7 years old came for short stature, everything is normal but Delayed bone age and normal velocity. What you will do?
OptD: Reassure it will catch the adult height
why_right: "Everything is normal" with delayed bone age and normal growth velocity is constitutional delay of growth and puberty. These children have remaining growth potential, enter puberty late and reach a normal adult height, so the management is reassurance and growth monitoring.
why_wrong_block:
A. Changing dairy intake does not alter a normal variant; diet matters only when there is undernutrition with falling velocity or weight loss.
B. Basic labs (CBC, U&E and similar) are a screen for chronic disease when velocity is slow or the child is unwell; with a normal exam and normal velocity they add nothing here.
C. Increasing sun exposure targets vitamin D deficiency rickets, which would show bony signs and poor growth, not a healthy child with normal velocity.
key_concept:
Short stature with normal height velocity = normal variant.
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, family history of late puberty, normal final height
  • Familial short stature: bone age = chronological age, ends short but on mid-parental target
  • Pathological: falling velocity, bone age delayed 2 years or more with low IGF-1 (think GH deficiency)
  • Mid-parental height best predicts final height
exam_pearl: Normal velocity is the reassurance clue; a falling velocity turns the same child into a workup.

stem: Baby had a delayed separation of his umbilical cords and start bleeding from the site. Labs of coagulation normal PT, PTT and platelets count and function normal. There is delay in clot time only. Which factors is affected? I think clot lysis time was 5 seconds (I don't care, I choose F-13 anyway as all other options are wrong)
highlight_terms_source: delayed separation of his umbilical cords
normal PT, PTT and platelets count and function
why_right: Bleeding from the umbilical stump with normal PT, PTT, platelet count and platelet function points to factor XIII deficiency. Factor XIII cross-links fibrin to stabilise the clot; it acts after the cascade measured by PT and PTT, so routine tests are normal while the formed clot is unstable (screen: clot dissolves in urea solution).
why_wrong_block:
A. Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) prolongs the aPTT and classically bleeds into joints or after circumcision; here the PTT is normal.
B. Von Willebrand disease gives mucosal bleeding with abnormal platelet function testing and often a prolonged aPTT; platelet function here is normal.
D. Thrombocytopenia is excluded by a normal platelet count and causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding rather than stump bleeding.
key_concept:
Bleeding with ALL screening tests normal: think factor XIII deficiency.
  • Clues: umbilical stump bleeding, delayed wound bleeding, intracranial bleed in infancy
  • Test: clot solubility in urea
  • aPTT only prolonged: VIII, IX, XI (XII without bleeding)
  • PT only prolonged: VII
  • PT and aPTT prolonged: X, V, II, fibrinogen
exam_pearl: Delayed cord SEPARATION without bleeding, with infections and neutrophilia, is leukocyte adhesion deficiency, not a coagulation defect.

  • Intubate and suction only if the airway is obstructed

stem: Newborn with respiratory distress covered with meconum he was on conventional ventilation then high flow ventilation what most effective managment for him ?
highlight_terms_source: conventional ventilation then high flow ventilation
key_concept:
Meconium aspiration not responding to ventilation = suspect PPHN.
  • Clue: pre-ductal saturation higher than post-ductal (right-to-left ductal shunt)
  • Confirm with echocardiography
  • Treatment: optimise ventilation and oxygen, then inhaled nitric oxide
  • Failure of iNO: ECMO
  • Surfactant can help by replacing surfactant inactivated by meconium
exam_pearl: A pre/post-ductal saturation gap in a ventilated meconium baby points straight to iNO.

stem: Picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia, the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue. CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC. What is the treatment?
why_right: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, lethargy and fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic CBC is iron deficiency anemia. The lead in asks for treatment, and the first line treatment of IDA in a child who can take tablets or syrup is oral ferrous sulfate. Response is checked by a rise in reticulocytes and hemoglobin after starting oral iron.
why_wrong_block:
A. Parenteral iron is reserved for failure of oral iron: malabsorption (e.g. celiac or IBD), true intolerance or persistent nonadherence. Nothing here suggests oral therapy has failed.
C. Folic acid deficiency gives a megaloblastic macrocytic anemia; this smear is microcytic and hypochromic.
D. B12 deficiency is also macrocytic and may bring neurological signs; it does not cause spoon nails or a microcytic picture.
key_concept:
Microcytic hypochromic anemia plus koilonychia = iron deficiency; treat with oral ferrous sulfate first.
  • IDA signs: pallor, fatigue, pica, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • IDA labs: low ferritin, MCV, MCH; high TIBC, RDW, platelets
  • High RDW favors IDA; normal RDW favors thalassemia trait
  • No response to adequate oral iron: think thalassemia, so do Hb electrophoresis
  • Parenteral iron only when oral fails or cannot be absorbed
exam_pearl: Microcytic anemia not improving on oral iron: check adherence and dosing first, then think thalassemia trait (normal RDW, do Hb electrophoresis); it is not an automatic switch to IV iron.

stem: Picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia, the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue. CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC. What is the Diagnosis?
why_right: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, lethargy and fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic film is the classic picture of iron deficiency anemia, the commonest anemia in children. Confirm with low ferritin and serum iron with high TIBC.
why_wrong_block: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a MACROcytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and possible neurological signs; it does not produce microcytosis or spoon nails.
key_concept:
Microcytic anemia: iron deficiency until proven otherwise.
  • IDA: low ferritin, low iron, high TIBC, high RDW, reactive thrombocytosis
  • Signs: koilonychia, pica, angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • Thalassemia trait: microcytosis with high RBC count, normal RDW, no response to iron
  • First line: oral ferrous sulfate
exam_pearl: Microcytosis that fails iron therapy with a high RBC count suggests thalassemia, not iron deficiency.

stem: Mile stone: A child accompanied by his parents walked into the examination room. He is holding a ball. The doctor asks to let him see the ball; he threw the ball towards the doctor. Then he reaches out to catch it when the doctor threw the ball back to him. He draws a straight line on the paper and then picks up a few blocks from the floor and stacks one on the top of the other. What is the most likely developmental month for this child?
highlight_terms_source: stacks one on the top of the other
why_right: The child throws a ball, reaches out to catch it, draws a line and stacks blocks. Stacking two cubes is a 15 month skill, but catching with extended hands is an 18 month skill, and throwing and line drawing push the child to the upper end; 18 months is the highest option consistent with all of them.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 9 months the child is sitting and pulling to stand with a pincer grasp developing; throwing, catching, drawing and stacking are far beyond this age.
B. At 12 months the child walks with one hand held and has a mature pincer grasp; stacking cubes (15 months) and catching (18 months) are not yet expected.
C. 15 months fits stacking two cubes, but catching with extended hands is an 18 month skill, so 15 underestimates this child.
key_concept:
Milestone questions: the most advanced skill sets the age.
  • 12 months: walks with one hand held, pincer grasp
  • 15 months: stacks 2 cubes, inserts pellet in bottle
  • 18 months: catches with extended hands
  • 2 years: throws overhand, copies lines
exam_pearl: Pick the age of the highest milestone the child shows, not the earliest one.

stem: baby with recurrent migraine for 2 weeks daily what to give given initial treatment with no effect what next?

  • Acute, moderate to severe: triptan

  • Prophylaxis options: beta blocker, amitriptyline (TCA), others
  • Daily analgesic use risks medication overuse headache

stem: baby 2 y with diarrhea. Mother concerned about her brother 1y/o How to prevent?
why_right: Infectious diarrhea in children spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route and close household contact, so the way to protect the "1y/o" brother is to interrupt transmission. Hand washing with soap (after diaper changes and toilet use, before preparing food and feeding) is the simplest and most effective preventive measure.
why_wrong_block: B. Prophylactic probiotics are not recommended to prevent transmission to contacts; probiotics are at most considered as an adjunct to shorten diarrhea in the affected child, not as household prevention.
key_concept:
Preventing spread of childhood diarrhea: break fecal-oral transmission.
  • Hand washing with soap: single best measure
  • Safe water and food hygiene
  • Proper diaper disposal, clean surfaces
  • Rotavirus vaccine for primary prevention in infants
  • Affected child: ORS and continue feeding
exam_pearl: "How to prevent" in a contact = hygiene, not a drug.

stem: A 5-week-old infant is brought by the mother after having sudden jerky movements involving upper and lower limbs. The infant was managed acutely with IV calcium. He is now stable and doing well. What is the most appropriate advice?
why_right: A "5-week-old" with jerky movements that needed "IV calcium" had a hypocalcemic seizure; in early infancy this is commonly due to vitamin D deficiency (often from a vitamin D deficient mother and exclusive breastfeeding). After acute correction, the underlying cause must be treated, so the advice is vitamin D supplementation (with calcium as needed) to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance alone ignores the cause; without vitamin D the hypocalcemia and seizures can recur. Reassurance fits benign events (e.g. normal newborn stool patterns), not a treated hypocalcemic seizure.
C. Avoiding sun is the opposite of what is needed: sunlight makes vitamin D in the skin. Sun avoidance is advised for photosensitive conditions, not for vitamin D deficiency.
key_concept:
Infant hypocalcemic seizure: correct calcium acutely, then treat the cause.
  • Common cause in early infancy: vitamin D deficiency (maternal deficiency, exclusive breastfeeding)
  • Nutritional vitamin D deficiency: low or normal Ca, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH, low 25-OH vitamin D
  • Prevention: routine vitamin D for breastfed infants (400 IU/day)
  • Also check and treat the mother
exam_pearl: Once the seizure is controlled, "most appropriate advice" targets the cause: vitamin D, not reassurance.

stem: Newborn in 3rd percentile, family poor was diluting formula milk, what is next most appropriate?
OptC: Advice family how to make formula
why_right: This recall's key is hospitalization: a newborn already at the "3rd percentile" with weight faltering from diluted formula has little reserve, and over-dilution also risks dilutional hyponatremia and seizures. With a "poor family" who may not be able to afford proper feeds, advice alone may fail, so admission allows supervised feeding, documentation of intake and weight gain, labs, and social work involvement.
why_wrong_block:
B. High-calorie formula treats inadequate calorie intake when the family feeds correctly, or when increased needs exist (e.g. cardiac disease); it does not fix the cause here (wrong preparation, poverty), and concentrated feeds in a newborn need supervision.
C. Teaching correct formula preparation is right when a stable infant with mild weight faltering has a simple preparation error and a family able to follow advice with close outpatient follow-up; the key here treats this newborn as needing admission first.
key_concept:
Failure to thrive from inadequate intake: decide outpatient vs inpatient.
  • Outpatient: mild, stable, reliable family, simple fixable cause (education, follow-up)
  • Admit: severe malnutrition, dehydration or electrolyte disturbance (diluted formula: hyponatremia), very young infant, failed outpatient care, neglect or safety concern
  • Always involve dietitian and social work when poverty drives the problem
exam_pearl: Diluted formula in a newborn can cause hyponatremic seizures, not just poor growth.

stem: Newborn with meconium aspiration syndrome has hypoxia and severe respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Intubation and mechanical ventilation if needed
why_right: Meconium aspiration syndrome with "hypoxia and severe respiratory distress" means respiratory failure. The newborn needs a secured airway with intubation and mechanical ventilation (plus surfactant and, if hypoxemia persists, inhaled nitric oxide or ECMO for pulmonary hypertension).
why_wrong_block: A. Supplemental oxygen with noninvasive positive pressure suits mild to moderate distress with adequate oxygenation; in severe MAS it is insufficient, and positive pressure without control can worsen air trapping and air leak (pneumothorax).
key_concept:
MAS management follows severity.
  • Mild: oxygen to target saturations, supportive care
  • Moderate: CPAP/noninvasive support with caution (air leak risk)
  • Severe or respiratory failure: intubation and mechanical ventilation
  • Adjuncts: surfactant, iNO for PPHN, HFOV, ECMO if refractory
  • Routine tracheal suctioning of non-vigorous infants is no longer recommended
exam_pearl: In a newborn with MAS, "severe" distress plus hypoxia = respiratory failure = intubate and ventilate; oxygen or CPAP is for milder cases.

  • Definitive: surgical repair at 3 to 6 months
  • Tet spell: knee to chest, oxygen, morphine, fluids, beta blocker

stem: 14-year-old male, diarrhea for 3 months, associated with abdominal bloating and loss of subcutaneous fat. What is the best treatment?
why_right: Chronic diarrhea ("3 months") with bloating and loss of subcutaneous fat (with a faltering growth chart) points to malabsorption, and in this setting celiac disease is the classic cause. Its treatment is a lifelong gluten free diet.
why_wrong_block:
A. A hydrolyzed (extensively hydrolyzed protein) diet is for cow's milk protein allergy, mainly in infants; not a 14-year-old with chronic malabsorption.
C. A high-calorie diet suits undernutrition from inadequate intake (e.g. marasmus); here the problem is malabsorption, so extra calories are lost unless gluten is removed.
D. A fat free diet does not treat celiac disease; fat restriction (with MCT) is used for conditions such as intestinal lymphangiectasia or chylous leaks, not gluten enteropathy.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: chronic diarrhea + bloating + poor growth/weight loss.
  • Initial test: IgA anti-tTG (with total IgA), anti-endomysial antibody
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy)
  • Keep gluten in the diet until testing is done
  • Associations: dermatitis herpetiformis, iron deficiency, type 1 diabetes
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten free diet
exam_pearl: Do not start the gluten free diet before serology and biopsy: it causes false negative results.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A growth chart image was shown with it (per recaller).

stem: Girl with webbed neck, short stature, broad chest and widely spaced nipples. What to do next?

  • Clues: short stature, webbed neck, low hairline, shield chest, widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, primary amenorrhea
  • Diagnosis: karyotype 45,X (or mosaic)
  • Screen: echo (coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve), renal US (horseshoe kidney), thyroid
  • Treatment: growth hormone, estrogen replacement
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to chromosomal analysis.
exam_pearl: Confirm before you treat: karyotype comes before growth hormone.

stem: Pediatric 13 years of age, chest pain and other cardiac symptoms (dyspnea on exertion), and ASO = 800. How long will he use penicillin?
why_right: A "13 years" old with cardiac symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea on exertion) and a high ASO (800) has rheumatic fever with carditis. Secondary prophylaxis for carditis without residual heart disease is 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer: 13 + 10 = 23 years, which is longer than 21.
why_wrong_block:
B. Age 21 would be the stopping point only if "until 21" were longer than 10 years, i.e. in younger children with carditis (or for rheumatic fever without carditis); here 10 years carries him to 23.
C. Age 15 gives only 2 years of prophylaxis, below even the minimum for rheumatic fever without carditis (5 years or until 21).
key_concept:
Secondary prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin, after the last attack): take whichever is LONGER.
  • No carditis: 5 years or until age 21
  • Carditis, no residual heart disease: 10 years or until age 21
  • Carditis with residual valvular disease: 10 years or until age 40, lifetime may be needed
exam_pearl: Always compute both (age + years vs the age cutoff) and pick the later one; residual valve disease pushes the cutoff to 40.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller forgot the last option. Answer bar: 23 years old.

stem: Baby (2 months old) was diagnosed with congenital heart disease came to the ER with bluish discoloration, the mother said he was crying. What will you do?
key_concept:
Cyanosis with crying in a CHD infant: calm and reassess first, escalate only if it persists.
  • Cyanosis worse with crying or feeding = classic tetralogy of Fallot picture
  • Tet spell first aid: calm baby, knee-chest position, oxygen
  • Persistent spell: sedation and further medical treatment, then urgent cardiology
  • Back to baseline after calming: home with cardiology follow-up
  • Cyanotic CHD: TOF, TGA, tricuspid atresia, truncus arteriosus
exam_pearl: Cyanosis that appears only with crying settles when the baby is calmed; cyanosis that persists after calming, oxygen and knee-chest position is a true spell that needs escalation.

stem: 7 year old child fully vaccinated fall in the park presented with clean and small wound. What to do?
why_right: A fully vaccinated 7-year-old with a clean, small wound needs no tetanus prophylaxis: his last tetanus-containing dose (DTaP at school entry in the national schedule) is well within the 10-year window that applies to clean minor wounds. So after simple wound cleaning, reassurance is all that is needed.
why_wrong_block:
B. A tetanus booster for a clean minor wound is given only if vaccination is incomplete/unknown or the last dose was over 10 years ago (over 5 years for a dirty or tetanus-prone wound); neither applies to this child.
C. Tetanus immunoglobulin is for tetanus-prone (dirty, deep, devitalised) wounds in a person with fewer than 3 doses or unknown vaccine history; a fully vaccinated child with a clean wound does not need it.
D. Vaccine plus immunoglobulin together is for a dirty or tetanus-prone wound in an incompletely or unknown immunised patient; it is excessive here.
key_concept:
Tetanus prophylaxis depends on wound type and vaccine history.
  • Clean minor wound, 3 or more doses: booster only if last dose over 10 years ago
  • Dirty/tetanus-prone wound, 3 or more doses: booster if last dose over 5 years ago
  • Fewer than 3 doses or unknown: give vaccine; add TIG only if wound is dirty/tetanus-prone
  • TIG is for exposure, never routine prevention
exam_pearl: Change the wound to dirty or the history to unknown/incomplete and the answer moves to vaccine, or vaccine plus TIG.

stem: 4-month child: delayed motor, hypotonia + reduced reflexes + antigravity muscles weak, CK normal, myopathic pattern on (EMG?).
