  • Congenital myopathy: reflexes reduced, CK normal or mildly raised, EMG myopathic, diagnosis by biopsy
  • Congenital muscular dystrophy: CK markedly raised, EMG myopathic, contractures common
  • Central (brain) hypotonia: reflexes normal or brisk, weakness less marked
exam_pearl: Normal CK plus myopathic EMG points to congenital myopathy; normal CK plus neurogenic EMG and fasciculations points to SMA.

stem: 6-year-old boy with day and night enuresis, his mother mentioned chronic constipation; exam is normal apart from sacral dimples. What should you do?
why_right: This is not simple bedwetting: the child has day and night enuresis plus chronic constipation and a sacral dimple, which together suggest a neurogenic bladder and bowel from occult spinal dysraphism (e.g. tethered cord). The enuresis work-up says daytime symptoms with constipation and a lumbosacral spine abnormality need MRI of the lumbosacral spine to detect a congenital spinal defect.
why_wrong_block:
B. Reassurance fits primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: night wetting only, no daytime symptoms, normal urinalysis and normal exam. Daytime wetting, constipation and a sacral marker rule that out here.
C. Urinalysis is done in every child with enuresis and is the key test when no red flag is present (it screens for UTI, diabetes and diabetes insipidus), but it cannot find the suspected spinal lesion; the sacral dimple with bladder and bowel dysfunction is the decisive finding.
key_concept:
Enuresis + constipation + spine marker = image the spine.
  • Every child: urinalysis
  • Night only, normal UA and exam: primary monosymptomatic enuresis, reassure
  • Daytime symptoms with constipation/encopresis: look for hypothyroidism, recurrent UTI, spine deformity
  • Recurrent UTI: renal ultrasound and VCUG
  • Lumbosacral deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
exam_pearl: Remove the sacral dimple and the daytime symptoms, and the answer becomes urinalysis or reassurance.

stem: A 6 month infant with vertical transmission of HIV, started on antiretroviral therapy and developmentally doing good. Which of the following vaccines needs to be considered?
key_concept:
HIV child: inactivated vaccines always; live vaccines only if not severely immunosuppressed.
  • Viral vaccines are live except hepatitis B, hepatitis A, IPV, HPV and inactivated influenza
  • Inactivated influenza: from 6 months, yearly, recommended in HIV
  • MMR and varicella: live, from 12 months, only with adequate CD4
  • BCG: avoided in HIV-infected infants
  • Hep B, DTaP, PCV, Hib: safe, give per schedule
exam_pearl: In an HIV-infected child, inactivated vaccines are always safe; the live ones (MMR, varicella, BCG) are the ones whose timing depends on age and CD4.

stem: 4 months old came with mild flu symptoms, T 37.1; mother asking about vaccinations?
key_concept:
Mild illness is not a contraindication; vaccinate on schedule.
  • Postpone only for moderate or severe acute illness
  • 2 and 4 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus
  • 6 months: OPV first appears, plus IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV13
  • 9 months: measles + MCV4
  • 18 months: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, varicella, Hep A
exam_pearl: Runny nose with normal temperature = vaccinate today; only a moderately to severely ill child has vaccines deferred.

stem: Gravida 41 weeks, child delivered via NVD and had respiratory distress but not saturated. What next?
why_right: A 41-week (late-term) newborn with respiratory distress who is not saturating is hypoxaemic, and the immediate step is supplemental oxygen titrated to target saturation while the cause (meconium aspiration is a concern at this gestation, or TTN) is worked out. Treat the hypoxia first, then investigate and escalate support if oxygen alone fails.
why_wrong_block:
B. Keeping the baby NPO is a reasonable supportive measure in a tachypnoeic neonate to reduce aspiration risk, but it does nothing for the low saturation and is not the next step.
C. Surfactant is for surfactant-deficient RDS in a preterm infant (and sometimes for severe meconium aspiration after intubation); it is not first-line for a term or post-term baby who has only just been started on support.
D. Magnesium sulfate is a maternal drug for preeclampsia/eclampsia and fetal neuroprotection; it has no role as the next step in a hypoxic newborn.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress with low saturation: oxygen first, then find the cause.
  • Preterm: RDS (surfactant deficiency), may need CPAP and surfactant
  • Term CS: TTN, self-resolving, supportive oxygen
  • Post-term, meconium-stained liquor: meconium aspiration syndrome
  • Escalate oxygen to CPAP/ventilation if saturation does not improve
exam_pearl: Surfactant is the trap: it belongs to the preterm RDS story, not to a 41-week baby whose first need is oxygen.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0237).

stem: A 2-month-old baby presented with fever, vomiting, lethargy, and poor oral intake for 2 days. Urine dipstick shows nitrites, leukocytes. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Send to hospital and start IV antibiotics
highlight_terms_source: fever, vomiting, lethargy, and poor oral intake
why_right: A 2-month-old with fever, vomiting, lethargy and poor intake plus nitrites and leukocytes has a febrile UTI (likely pyelonephritis, possibly urosepsis). Age under 3 months, a toxic or lethargic appearance and inability to keep oral intake down are each indications for admission and IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block: A. Oral antibiotics at home suit an older, well-looking child who tolerates oral intake; this young, lethargic, vomiting infant may not absorb oral drugs and is at risk of sepsis, so outpatient oral treatment is unsafe.
key_concept:
Paediatric UTI: admit for IV antibiotics when the child is young or unwell.
  • Age under 3 months
  • Toxic, lethargic or septic appearance
  • Vomiting or unable to tolerate oral intake
  • Otherwise well older child: oral antibiotics as outpatient
  • Send urine culture before starting antibiotics
exam_pearl: Any febrile UTI under 3 months is managed in hospital with IV antibiotics, however well the dipstick story looks.

stem: Post term has respiratory distress and shifted to NICU. X-ray: patchy, bilateral infiltrates, hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, increased AP diameter, pneumomediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A post-term baby with respiratory distress whose X-ray shows patchy bilateral infiltrates with hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms and an air leak (pneumomediastinum) has meconium aspiration syndrome. Meconium causes patchy atelectasis and ball-valve airway obstruction, giving air trapping and air leaks; post-maturity is the main risk factor.
why_wrong_block: A. TTN is a term (usually CS) baby with mild, self-resolving tachypnoea and perihilar streaks with fluid in the fissures on X-ray; patchy infiltrates with air leak in a post-term baby admitted to NICU point to meconium aspiration instead.
key_concept:
Neonatal distress: gestation plus X-ray picks the diagnosis.
  • Preterm (or term with maternal diabetes): RDS, ground-glass reticulogranular pattern, low volumes
  • Term CS: TTN, perihilar streaks, fluid in fissures, resolves
  • Post-term, meconium-stained liquor: MAS, patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, air leaks
exam_pearl: Post-term + patchy infiltrates + hyperinflation or pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum = meconium aspiration.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall (screenshot): 'A newborn with RD on X-ray: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm and pneumomediastinum' A-RDS B-MAS C-TE fistula D-TTN. Compiler: Poor recall, both A & D are correct; however if he is pre-term (or term with C-section + maternal diabetes) -> RDS; post-term -> MAS.

stem: Newborn of mother known case of GDM was in distress, born through CS around 37-39 weeks, found to have pneumomediastinum and increased AP diameter with flattened diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is RDS because of the risk-factor pattern: a mother with GDM (fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant maturation) and delivery by CS around early term, so surfactant deficiency can occur even near term. Meconium aspiration is not offered, and air leak (pneumomediastinum) is a recognised complication of RDS, especially once ventilated.
why_wrong_block:
A. TTN is the classic term CS baby with mild, self-limiting tachypnoea and fluid in the fissures; here maternal diabetes, which delays lung maturity, is the clue the key uses to choose RDS over TTN.
C. Tracheoesophageal fistula presents with frothy secretions, choking and cyanosis with feeds and failure to pass a nasogastric tube (coiled on X-ray), not with distress plus hyperinflation at birth.
key_concept:
Risk factor sorts the neonatal distress question.
  • Preterm, or early-term with maternal diabetes (especially by CS): RDS (surfactant deficiency)
  • Term CS without other risk: TTN
  • Post-term: meconium aspiration syndrome
  • RDS X-ray: ground-glass, air bronchograms, low lung volumes
  • TTN X-ray: perihilar streaks, fissural fluid, may be hyperinflated
exam_pearl: Maternal diabetes is the clue examiners use to turn a near-term CS baby from TTN into RDS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No meconium aspiration syndrome in choices. Compiler: pre-term (or term with C-section + maternal diabetes) -> RDS; post-term -> MAS.

stem: 6-week-old infant, currently below the 3rd percentile for weight, presents with stridor that worsens when supine and improves when prone. The infant also experiences apneic episodes and abnormal breathing sounds. Clinical suspicion is high for laryngomalacia. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: stridor that worsens when supine and improves when prone
why_right: Positional stridor that is worse supine and better prone fits laryngomalacia, which is usually self-limiting. But this infant has red flags of severe disease: weight "below the 3rd percentile" (failure to thrive) and "apneic episodes". Severe laryngomalacia needs ENT referral for laryngoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and assess for surgery (supraglottoplasty), so referral is the most appropriate next step.
why_wrong_block:
B. Reassure the parents: right for mild laryngomalacia with normal growth and no apnea, which resolves by 1 to 2 years. Failure to thrive and apnea rule out simple reassurance here.
C. Start bronchodilators: laryngomalacia is a structural floppiness of the supraglottic larynx, not bronchospasm, so bronchodilators do nothing. They suit wheeze from asthma, not inspiratory stridor.
D. Order a chest X-ray: does not show the larynx or confirm laryngomalacia. Diagnosis is by direct laryngoscopy, done by ENT.
key_concept:
Laryngomalacia: worse supine, better prone; severity decides management.
  • Mild (normal growth, no apnea): reassure, resolves by 1 to 2 years
  • Severe (failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty): refer ENT
  • Diagnosis: laryngoscopy
  • Tracheomalacia: noise disappears supine; diagnosed by bronchoscopy
exam_pearl: Same positional stridor: normal growth = reassure; failure to thrive or apnea = refer ENT.

stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother, who is concerned about potential exposure to gastroenteritis after the infant's older sister was diagnosed several days ago. The infant is currently well-appearing and up to date on vaccinations. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
OptD: Reassure the mother and monitor for symptoms
highlight_terms_source: well-appearing and up to date on vaccinations
why_right: The infant is "well-appearing" and "up to date on vaccinations", so at 3 months she has already had her first rotavirus dose (given at 2 months). There is no post-exposure prophylaxis for viral gastroenteritis, so the correct advice is reassurance and watching for symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea and signs of dehydration, with good hand hygiene at home.
why_wrong_block:
A. Encourage increased free water intake: a 3-month-old should get breast milk or formula only; extra free water risks hyponatremia. If diarrhea develops, oral rehydration solution is used, not plain water.
B. Administer the rotavirus vaccine: she is already up to date, and rotavirus vaccine is given on schedule, not as post-exposure prophylaxis. It would be right only for a missed scheduled dose within the age window.
C. Discontinue fruit juice at dinner: a 3-month-old should not be taking juice at all, and stopping juice does not prevent infection. Juice restriction matters for toddler's diarrhea, not exposure.
key_concept:
Well infant exposed to gastroenteritis: reassure and monitor.
  • No post-exposure prophylaxis for viral gastroenteritis
  • Rotavirus is the only common viral cause with a vaccine; given on schedule from 2 months
  • If symptoms start: oral rehydration solution and continued feeding
  • Under 6 months: no free water or juice
exam_pearl: "Up to date on vaccinations" means rotavirus is already given; do not re-vaccinate after exposure.

stem: A child presents with recurrent infections including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections, and his mother confirmed he had episodes of diarrhea. Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: recurrent infections including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections
why_right: Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections ("pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections") plus chronic "diarrhea" are the typical pattern of a humoral (antibody) immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, CVID or IgA deficiency (often with Giardia diarrhea). The first screening test for suspected antibody deficiency is serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM).
why_wrong_block:
A. Check C1 inhibitor levels: tests for hereditary angioedema (recurrent non-itchy swelling, abdominal attacks), not recurrent infections.
B. Hemolytic complement (CH50): screens for complement deficiency, classically recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections or lupus-like disease. It is a second-line test once immunoglobulins are normal, not the first screen for sinopulmonary infections with diarrhea.
C. Thrombocytopenia: a finding, not an investigation. Low platelets with eczema and infections would point to Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, which is not described here.
key_concept:
Match infection pattern to the immune arm and its first test.
  • Recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections ± diarrhea: antibody defect → serum immunoglobulins
  • Recurrent Neisseria: complement → CH50
  • Fungal, viral, opportunistic: T-cell defect → lymphocyte count / subsets
  • Catalase-positive abscesses: phagocyte defect (CGD) → neutrophil function test
  • Recurrent swelling without urticaria: C1 inhibitor
exam_pearl: Sinopulmonary infections plus Giardia-type diarrhea = antibody deficiency; start with immunoglobulin levels.

stem: 5 year Down syndrome, came with diarrhea and irritability.
why_right: Down syndrome carries a higher risk of autoimmune thyroid disease, including Graves hyperthyroidism as well as hypothyroidism. "Diarrhea and irritability" are typical hyperthyroid features (increased gut motility, restlessness), so thyroid function tests are the right investigation. Thyroid screening is also part of routine Down syndrome follow-up.
why_wrong_block: B. US Abdomen: suits a structural or surgical cause (mass, intussusception, obstruction), but there is no pain, mass or vomiting here. Irritability with diarrhea points to a systemic, endocrine cause.
key_concept:
Down syndrome conditions to screen for when new symptoms appear:
  • Thyroid disease (congenital hypothyroidism, later Hashimoto or Graves): TFTs
  • Celiac disease: tTG-IgA with total IgA
  • Duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease (neonatal)
  • AVSD (most common heart defect)
  • Leukemia; atlantoaxial instability
exam_pearl: Diarrhea in Down syndrome has two main suspects: hyperthyroidism (irritable, restless) and celiac disease (poor growth, bloating); check which test the options offer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: He doesn't remember if celiac was present or not. Not sure if presence of celiac would change the answer. Diarrhea + mood changes (irritability) = think of HYPER-thyroidism. Does Down predispose to hyperthyroidism? (Know hypo, not sure of hyper; did not search for it.)

stem: 8 years old boy presented with focal pain on his left leg that is increasing in intensity, associated with local warmth and tenderness and subjective fever. He has a history of fall with wound. What is the radiological investigation for the leg?
highlight_terms_source: focal pain on his left leg
local warmth and tenderness and subjective fever
why_right: Increasing focal pain with "local warmth and tenderness" and fever after a fall with a wound in a child suggests acute osteomyelitis. This recall's key is MRI because it is the most sensitive and specific imaging for osteomyelitis: it shows marrow edema within days and detects subperiosteal abscess, while plain films stay normal for about the first 10 to 14 days.
why_wrong_block:
A. X ray: usually done first as a baseline to exclude fracture or foreign body, but early osteomyelitis looks normal on X-ray; bone changes appear only after 1 to 2 weeks. It is the answer if the question asks for the initial study.
C. CT scan: shows cortical bone and sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis but is poor for early marrow changes and exposes the child to radiation.
D. Nuclear scan: sensitive bone scan useful when the site is unclear or multifocal, or when MRI is unavailable; less specific than MRI and gives no anatomy of abscesses.
key_concept:
Imaging in pediatric acute osteomyelitis:
  • X-ray: first-line baseline, normal early
  • MRI: investigation of choice (most sensitive and specific)
  • Bone scan: site unclear or multifocal, MRI unavailable
  • Ultrasound: joint effusion or subperiosteal collection
  • Diagnosis confirmed by blood culture or bone aspirate
exam_pearl: "Initial" imaging = X-ray; "best" or "most sensitive" imaging = MRI.

stem: 6 y old boy presents with convulsions, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, Hb and plt low, WBCs 25. What is the line of management for his CNS, should it be involved?
why_right: Pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, low Hb and platelets with a high WBC in a 6-year-old is acute leukemia (most likely ALL), and "convulsions" raise concern for CNS involvement. Most systemic chemotherapy does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so CNS leukemia is treated (and prevented) with intrathecal chemotherapy, typically methotrexate, given into the CSF.
why_wrong_block:
A. Systemic chemotherapy: the backbone treatment for the leukemia overall, but standard IV drugs reach the CSF poorly, so on its own it does not control CNS disease.
C. Anticonvulsant: controls the seizures symptomatically but does not treat the leukemic infiltration that is causing them.
D. Ventriculopleural shunt: a CSF diversion for hydrocephalus; it does not treat CNS leukemia and is not part of its management.
key_concept:
Childhood ALL and the CNS:
  • Features: pallor, bleeding, infections, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
  • Diagnosis: bone marrow aspiration
  • CNS is a sanctuary site because of the blood-brain barrier
  • CNS prophylaxis and treatment: intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate)
  • Cranial irradiation is reserved for selected high-risk cases
exam_pearl: CNS is a sanctuary site in ALL: the treatment goes into the CSF (intrathecal), not just the vein.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Explanation linked externally (Telegram).

stem: X ray I think it was boot shape heart of 6 days old child with sx of cyanosis, ask abt most important management at this age I remember 2
why_right: A "boot shape heart" with cyanosis is Tetralogy of Fallot. In a cyanotic "6 days old" newborn, pulmonary blood flow may depend on the ductus arteriosus, which is closing in the first days of life. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct open and maintains pulmonary flow until definitive repair, so it is the most important management at this age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiac catheterization: TOF is diagnosed by echocardiography; catheterization is not needed for diagnosis and is not the urgent step in a cyanotic neonate. It has a role in selected anatomy or interventions later.
C. Elective surgical repair: this is the definitive treatment, usually at 3 to 6 months of age, but it is not the immediate step for a cyanotic 6-day-old whose ductus is closing.
key_concept:
Cyanotic newborn with suspected duct-dependent CHD: start PGE1 first.
  • TOF CXR: boot shaped heart, reduced pulmonary markings
  • TOF confirmatory test: echocardiography
  • TOF definitive repair: 3 to 6 months
  • Tet spell: knee to chest, oxygen, morphine, IV fluids, beta blocker
  • TGA CXR: egg on a string; also PGE1 first
exam_pearl: Newborn cyanotic CHD = PGE1 first; elective repair is the answer only when asked for definitive treatment.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Image caption: Boot shaped heart = TOF.

stem: A 4 month old baby with cough, running nose, nasal flaring, increase work of breathing with no fever, on examination expiratory wheeze in all lower lung zones and suprasternal retraction. What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: expiratory wheeze in all lower lung zones
why_right: A "4 month old" with upper airway symptoms (cough, "running nose") followed by lower airway signs (diffuse "expiratory wheeze", nasal flaring, retractions) is the classic picture of bronchiolitis, usually from RSV. Low grade or absent fever fits, and it is a clinical diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumonia: usually brings fever, focal crackles or reduced breath sounds and focal consolidation, not diffuse wheeze in all lung zones.
C. Bronchial asthma: needs recurrent episodes and is not diagnosed in a 4-month-old with a first wheezy illness after a cold; it suits an older child with recurrent wheeze and atopy.
D. Viral croup: an upper airway illness of 6 months to 3 years with barking cough and inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheeze.
key_concept:
Infant wheeze after a cold = bronchiolitis.
  • Age under 2 years (peak under 1 year); RSV most common
  • URTI (coryza, cough) then LRTI (wheeze, crackles, retractions)
  • Clinical diagnosis; CXR not routine
  • Treatment supportive: oxygen and hydration
  • Croup: barking cough + inspiratory stridor; asthma: recurrent wheeze in older child
exam_pearl: Expiratory wheeze = lower airway (bronchiolitis); inspiratory stridor with barking cough = upper airway (croup).

stem: Woman with known chronic hepatitis B infection delivers a healthy newborn. The infant receives hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth. What to give?
OptB: Second dose of hepatitis B vaccine
why_right: A baby born to a mother with "chronic hepatitis B" (HBsAg-positive) needs both active and passive immunization. The vaccine has already been given, so the missing piece is hepatitis B immunoglobulin, ideally within 12 hours of birth, to sharply reduce vertical transmission.
why_wrong_block: B. Second dose of hepatitis B vaccine: the series continues on schedule at 1 to 2 months, not immediately. It does not replace HBIG, which gives the immediate passive protection the vaccine alone cannot.
key_concept:
Newborn of HBsAg-positive mother:
  • Hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth
  • Complete the vaccine series on schedule
  • Test the infant for HBsAg and anti-HBs after the series
  • Breastfeeding is not contraindicated
exam_pearl: Mother HBsAg-positive: vaccine alone is not enough; add HBIG within 12 hours.

stem: A newborn presents with ambiguous genitalia and clitoromegaly. Laboratory findings show hyponatremia, hyperkalemia. The 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is elevated. What is the most appropriate initial/next management?
why_right: Ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly, raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone, "hyponatremia, hyperkalemia" is salt-wasting CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The electrolyte picture signals an adrenal crisis that can lead to shock, so the most appropriate initial management is IV hydrocortisone with IV fluid (saline) resuscitation, adding glucose if hypoglycemic.
why_wrong_block: A. Karyotyping & ultrasound: needed to confirm genetic sex and internal anatomy in ambiguous genitalia, but they do not treat a life-threatening salt-wasting crisis. They are the answer for a stable baby with ambiguous genitalia and normal electrolytes.
key_concept:
Salt-wasting CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency):
  • Girls: ambiguous genitalia; boys: may present only with crisis at 1 to 3 weeks
  • Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, shock
  • Diagnosis: raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone
  • Acute: IV hydrocortisone + saline (+ glucose if low)
  • Long term: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone; autosomal recessive
exam_pearl: Abnormal electrolytes turn "workup" into "resuscitate": stabilize first, karyotype later.

stem: A 5-year-old girl's mother noticed two episodes of night bedwetting, starting after the birth of her sister. She remains dry in the evening.
highlight_terms_source: after the birth of her sister
why_right: This is secondary enuresis in a 5-year-old: she was previously dry, wetting started after a clear stressor ("after the birth of her sister") and there have been only two episodes. A short, stress-related regression like this is managed first with reassurance and simple behavioural measures, of which restricting evening fluids (plus voiding before bed and avoiding blame) is the practical first step.
why_wrong_block: A. Psychiatric evaluation is excessive for two wetting episodes clearly linked to a new sibling; it is considered only if there are persistent behavioural or emotional problems, or signs of abuse or major family stress.
key_concept:
Enuresis: rule out organic causes, then behavioural measures first.
  • Primary: never dry for 6 months; usually maturational, often familial
  • Secondary: wetting after a dry period; look for stressor, UTI, diabetes, constipation
  • Simple check: urinalysis (glucose, infection)
  • First line: reassurance, evening fluid limit, void before bed, reward chart
  • Persistent cases: enuresis alarm (most effective long term), desmopressin for short-term control
exam_pearl: New sibling + brief regression = behavioural measures, not a psychiatry referral; polyuria, daytime wetting or dysuria would instead demand urinalysis and work-up.

stem: Pediatric patient presented in ER with fever and barky cough a long senario but he was in distress Bp was 80/60, Oxygen was 80% What is the appropriate initial management?
OptC: Some type of intubation in the OR
key_concept:
Barky cough + distress: grade severity, then treat the airway.
  • Mild croup (no stridor at rest): single dose dexamethasone
  • Moderate/severe (stridor at rest, retractions): nebulized epinephrine + steroid + oxygen
  • Impending failure (hypoxia, fatigue, altered consciousness): secure airway
  • Toxic, high fever, drooling, tripod: epiglottitis, prepare for intubation + 3rd generation cephalosporin
  • Toxic with barky cough not responding to epinephrine: bacterial tracheitis
exam_pearl: SpO2 80% is never plain mild croup: oxygen and airway assessment come first, then look for severe croup versus a bacterial airway infection.

Compiler note: No answer marked for this severe version.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 2 y Pediatric patient presented in ER with low grade fever and (brassy cough!) not barky. What is the appropriate initial management?
why_right: A 2-year-old with low grade fever and a croupy cough, with no stridor at rest and no hypoxia mentioned, has mild croup. Dexamethasone is the primary treatment of croup at every severity, and for mild disease a single dose of dexamethasone alone is the appropriate initial management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cool humidified air is a traditional home measure without proven benefit; it does not replace a steroid dose.
B. Prednisolone is an acceptable alternative steroid, but dexamethasone is preferred because it is longer acting, given once and best supported by evidence.
D. Racemic epinephrine is reserved for moderate to severe croup (stridor at rest, retractions, distress); it acts fast but briefly and is not needed in mild croup.
key_concept:
Croup treatment follows severity.
  • Cause: parainfluenza virus; clinical diagnosis (steeple sign if X-ray done)
  • Mild: dexamethasone single dose, home
  • Moderate/severe: nebulized epinephrine + dexamethasone, observe for rebound
  • Epinephrine may be repeated if no response
  • No antibiotics, antihistamines or bronchodilators
exam_pearl: Stridor at rest or retractions flips the answer to racemic epinephrine (plus steroid); without them, steroid alone.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: 'Q: Mild symptoms clear question?' (typed options Dexa 0.6 / Prednisone / Racemic epinephrine). Screenshot marks D racemic epinephrine, but compiler: now we have the full recall; stridor not mentioned, hypoxia not mentioned, mild retractions, stem INITIAL. This is MILD croup, epinephrine is NOT needed; answer is Dexa (all are steroids). Another version (2 y male, low grade fever, brassy cough and inspiratory stridor, most appropriate management; humidified air / prednisone 2.5 / dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg / racemic epinephrine): answer to this specific recall remains C.
Other marked answers: Screenshot: D. racemic epinephrine

stem: A 9-month-old boy presents to the clinic with skin rash noticed by his parent over the past few weeks. His parents are known to have eczema before. Which of the following is the typical site of eczematous plaques at this age?
why_right: In a 9-month-old with an atopic family history, infantile eczema classically involves the face and head: scalp, cheeks and forehead. From about 6 months extensor surfaces join the face, but of these options the facial/scalp pattern is the typical infant site.
why_wrong_block:
A. The upper back is not a classic site of infant eczema; at this age the face, scalp and extensor surfaces of the limbs are typical, with flexures taking over after 2 years.
B. The diaper area is typically spared in atopic eczema because the skin stays moist; a diaper rash suggests irritant or candidal dermatitis.
C. The dorsum of the feet is not the typical infant site; the face, scalp and extensor surfaces are.
key_concept:
Eczema distribution changes with age.
  • <6 months: face, head, scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexures (antecubital, popliteal)
  • >12 years: flexures and perioral region
  • Treatment: emollients, non-soap cleansers, topical steroids
exam_pearl: Infant eczema spares the diaper area; a rash there points away from atopic dermatitis.

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents to the clinic with skin rash noticed by his parent over the past few weeks. His parents are known to have eczema before. Which of the following is the typical site of eczematous plaques at this age?
why_right: An 8-year-old falls in the childhood (2 to 12 years) phase of atopic eczema, which classically affects the flexural creases, especially the antecubital and popliteal fossae.
why_wrong_block:
A. The upper back is not a characteristic eczema site in childhood.
B. The dorsal feet are not the typical childhood site; dorsal foot dermatitis in a child raises shoe contact dermatitis.
D. Scalp, cheeks and forehead are the infant pattern, not that of a school-age child.
key_concept:
Eczema distribution changes with age.
  • <6 months: face, head, scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexures (antecubital, popliteal)
  • >12 years: flexures and perioral region
exam_pearl: Same stem, different age: infant = face/scalp, child = flexures, adolescent = flexures plus perioral.

stem: A 14-year-old boy presents to the clinic with skin rash noticed by his parent over the past few weeks. His parents are known to have eczema before. Which of the following is the typical site of eczematous plaques at this age?
why_right: This recall's key follows the age table for eczema: after 12 years eczema involves flexural surfaces and the perioral region. For a 14-year-old, the site that distinguishes the adolescent pattern from the 2 to 12 year group is the perioral region.
why_wrong_block:
A. The popliteal fossa is the hallmark site of the 2 to 12 year phase; it can persist at 14, but it does not define the adolescent pattern the key asks for.
C. The antecubital fossa is likewise the hallmark 2 to 12 year flexural site; it is not the site specific to adolescence.
D. Scalp and forehead are the infantile pattern.
key_concept:
Eczema distribution changes with age.
  • <6 months: face, head, scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexures (antecubital, popliteal)
  • >12 years: flexures and perioral region (also face, neck, hands)
exam_pearl: Age pattern: popliteal/antecubital = 2 to 12 years, perioral = adolescent; when the question asks for the age-typical site, pick the age-specific one.

stem: down$ (didn't say down) depressed nasal bridge and Single Palmar Crease.
why_right: A depressed (flat) nasal bridge and single palmar crease are dysmorphic features of Down syndrome. The most common endocrine disorder in trisomy 21 is hypothyroidism (congenital or acquired, mostly autoimmune), which is why these children have repeated thyroid screening.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia is the classic endocrine feature of DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome, not Down syndrome.
C. Hypopituitarism is not a characteristic association of trisomy 21; it goes with midline defects such as septo-optic dysplasia.
D. Hyperthyroidism (Graves) is more frequent in Down syndrome than in the general population but far less common than hypothyroidism.
key_concept:
Down syndrome: recognize the face, then screen the associations.
  • Features: upslanting eyes, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, hypotonia
  • Heart: endocardial cushion (AVSD) defect most typical
  • Endocrine: hypothyroidism most common
  • Also: duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung, leukaemia, atlantoaxial instability, early Alzheimer
exam_pearl: Hypoparathyroidism is the DiGeorge trap; Down syndrome = hypothyroid.

stem: A child born post term, what is the neonatologist expected to find most in the baby?
why_right: A post-term baby has lost the protective vernix and is exposed to placental insufficiency, so the classic finding is dry, peeling, cracked, wrinkled skin (postmaturity or dysmaturity). This is the feature most expected on examination.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lanugo (fine body hair) is abundant in preterm babies and is largely shed by term; a post-term baby has little or none.
B. Placental insufficiency in postmaturity causes loss of subcutaneous fat and a wasted look; macrosomia can occur, but increased body fat is not the characteristic finding.
D. Post-term babies have long fingernails; short nails suggest prematurity.
key_concept:
Preterm vs post-term newborn signs.
  • Preterm: abundant lanugo, thin translucent skin, short nails, few sole creases
  • Post-term: dry peeling skin, little vernix and lanugo, long nails, alert wasted look
  • Post-term risks: meconium staining and aspiration, oligohydramnios, hypoglycaemia
exam_pearl: Lanugo and short nails point to preterm; dry peeling skin and long nails point to post-term.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer Is "Dry, Peeling, Wrinkled Skin" A Complication Of Post-Maturity (Specially To Diabetic Mothers)

stem: A baby boy received a vaccine and, after 3 days, developed a torso rash with mild fever (38.5 °C). He is otherwise well, tolerating oral intake, and physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
key_concept:
Post-vaccine rash: match timing and vaccine type.
  • Minutes to hours, urticaria or angioedema: allergy or anaphylaxis
  • 1 to 2 days after inactivated vaccine: fever, local reaction
  • About 1 to 2 weeks after MMR, up to about 3 to 4 weeks after varicella: fever and rash from the live virus
  • Mild reaction or fever after a dose is not a contraindication to the next dose
  • Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is an absolute contraindication
exam_pearl: Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is the key absolute contraindication; mild fever and rash after a dose do not stop future doses.

stem: 3 Years Old Post TEF Repair, Present With Brassy Cough, 2 Days Earlier He Had Runny Nose, Normal Vitals, Good Air Entry Bilaterally With Expiratory Wheeze?
why_right: Tracheomalacia is the expected sequela of TEF repair: the trachea at the fistula site has weak cartilage and collapses on expiration, giving the classic brassy cough and expiratory wheeze. A simple viral cold ("runny nose 2 days earlier") makes it more noticeable, while the child stays well with normal vitals and good air entry.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asthma gives recurrent episodic wheeze with atopy and response to bronchodilators; it does not explain a brassy cough tied to a repaired TEF.
C. Croup gives a barking cough with inspiratory stridor, hoarseness and often fever and distress after a coryzal prodrome; here the noise is expiratory and the child is stable.
key_concept:
Post-TEF repair + brassy cough + expiratory wheeze = tracheomalacia.
  • Tracheomalacia: dynamic collapse of intrathoracic trachea, expiratory noise; diagnosis by bronchoscopy
  • Laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor in early infancy, worse supine and with feeding; laryngoscopy
  • Croup: barky cough, inspiratory stridor, 6 months to 3 years
  • Other post-TEF problems: anastomotic stricture (dysphagia), recurrent fistula (cough with feeds), GERD
exam_pearl: Inspiratory stridor points above the thoracic inlet (larynx, croup); expiratory wheeze with brassy cough after TEF points to intrathoracic tracheomalacia.

stem: A child following up for being tall, has high arm span and long fingers, following up with ophthalmology for eye issues (written like this), no mental retardation. Most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: high arm span and long fingers
why_right: Tall stature, long arm span and long fingers (arachnodactyly) with eye problems needing ophthalmology follow up (myopia, ectopia lentis) and normal intelligence is Marfan syndrome. Normal cognition is what separates it from homocystinuria, which has a similar marfanoid body.
why_wrong_block:
B. Homocystinuria gives a marfanoid habitus with lens dislocation too, but adds intellectual disability and thrombosis; this child has no mental retardation.
C. Loeys-Dietz causes aortic aneurysms with hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate and arterial tortuosity; lens dislocation is not a feature, so the eye clue does not fit.
D. Ehlers-Danlos gives skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and easy bruising; it is not defined by tall stature, long arm span or lens problems.
key_concept:
Marfanoid body: sort by eye and IQ.
  • Marfan: autosomal dominant, FBN1; upward lens dislocation, myopia, aortic root dilation, MVP, normal IQ
  • Homocystinuria: autosomal recessive; downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, thrombosis
  • Loeys-Dietz: hypertelorism, bifid uvula, arterial tortuosity, aggressive aneurysms
  • Ehlers-Danlos: stretchy skin, hypermobile joints, poor wound healing
exam_pearl: Marfanoid child plus intellectual disability or thrombosis flips the answer to homocystinuria.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Tall stature + no eye symptoms = EDS; tall stature + eye symptoms = Marfan; tall stature + eye symptoms + retardation = Homocystinuria.

stem: 7-month-old pt. His mother noticed that he stopped smiling, low activity, fatigue. On examination he had multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting 1-2 seconds in a repetitive pattern. EEG showed slow wave & multifocal spikes (not sure, but it wasn't hypsarrhythmia or chaotic pattern). What's the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting 1-2 seconds
why_right: A 7-month-old with developmental regression ("stopped smiling", low activity) and brief repetitive flexion then extension spasms of neck, trunk and limbs lasting 1 to 2 seconds in clusters is infantile spasms (West syndrome). The EEG described, slow waves with multifocal spikes, is in fact what hypsarrhythmia consists of, so even an imperfect recall fits the triad of spasms, regression and abnormal EEG.
why_wrong_block:
A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks of the arms and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, normal development and generalized polyspike-wave EEG; it does not occur at 7 months.
C. Lennox-Gastaut presents later (usually 1 to 8 years) with multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absence), intellectual disability and slow spike-wave EEG; West syndrome often evolves into it.
key_concept:
Infant + clustered flexor/extensor spasms + regression = West syndrome.
  • Age: peak 4 to 8 months
  • Triad: infantile spasms, developmental arrest/regression, hypsarrhythmia
  • Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal spikes
  • Look for tuberous sclerosis (ash leaf spots, Wood lamp)
  • Treatment: ACTH or high-dose steroids; vigabatrin first line in tuberous sclerosis
  • Lennox-Gastaut: childhood, multiple seizure types, slow spike-wave
exam_pearl: Same spasms in a teenager on waking are myoclonic jerks (JME); age is the first clue in childhood epilepsy syndromes.

stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby with pancytopenia and organomegaly. Labs show low hemoglobin. What is the most likely type of leukemia?
why_right: A child with pancytopenia, organomegaly and low hemoglobin has bone marrow replacement with extramedullary infiltration, typical of acute leukemia. ALL is the most common childhood leukemia (and the most common childhood cancer), so it is the most likely type.
why_wrong_block:
A. AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
B. CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
D. Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.
key_concept:
Child + pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy = think acute leukemia; ALL is the most common.
  • ALL: most common childhood leukemia, peak in early childhood
  • AML (= acute non-lymphoblastic): second most common
  • CML: rare in children
exam_pearl: 'Acute non-lymphoblastic' is just AML in old wording; do not treat it as a separate answer.

stem: A 3-year-old child is seen in the clinic with fever and cough for 5 days following a flu-like prodrome. On examination, there is decreased air entry and crackles over the right lung middle zone. Chest X-ray is performed along with laboratory investigations. BP 90/64 mmHg, HR 110/min, RR 20/min, Temp 36.6 °C, SpO2 97%. Labs: Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 328 x10^9/L, WBC 22 x10^9/L, neutrophils 84%, lymphocytes 15%. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: crackles over the right lung middle zone
why_right: Fever and cough for 5 days with focal crackles and reduced air entry over the right middle zone, WBC 22 with 84% neutrophils, is bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, which needs antibiotics. The child is stable: SpO2 97%, normal RR and BP, no distress, so it is mild pneumonia managed at home with oral amoxicillin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits a viral URTI; focal chest signs with neutrophilic leukocytosis mean bacterial pneumonia that needs antibiotics.
B. Bronchodilator and steroids treat asthma or wheeze; this child has focal crackles, not diffuse wheeze.
C. Admission for IV antibiotics is for severe pneumonia: SpO2 below 92%, respiratory distress, tachypnea, inability to take oral fluids, toxic look or complications such as empyema; none are present.
key_concept:
Pediatric CAP: severity decides where and how.
  • Mild (well, SpO2 ≥92%, feeding): oral amoxicillin at home
  • Severe: hypoxia, grunting, retractions, poor feeding, toxicity: admit, IV antibiotics, oxygen
  • First-line oral drug: amoxicillin (covers pneumococcus)
  • Stony dullness suggests parapneumonic effusion
exam_pearl: Hypoxia (SpO2 below 92%) is the single sign that flips management from oral home treatment to admission.
